## 1.3. Eligibility to the centralised procedure

The applicant Sanofi Winthrop Industrie submitted on 10 October 2025 an application for marketing authorisation to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for VaxRabeo (Rabies vaccine (inactivated) for human use), through the centralised procedure under Article 28 of Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006. The eligibility to the centralised procedure was agreed upon by the EMA/CHMP on 30 May 2024.

The applicant applied for the following indication:

\"VaxRabeo is indicated for pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis against rabies in all age groups.

VaxRabeo should be used in accordance with official recommendations.\"

## 1.4. Legal basis and dossier content

## The legal basis for this application refers to:

Article 8.3 of Directive 2001/83/EC - complete and independent application

## 2. Introduction

## 2.1. Therapeutic context

## Disease or condition

Rabies is a serious public health concern and is one of the most common fatal infections worldwide. Rabies has the highest human case-fatality ratio of all infectious diseases. It is an acute neurological viral infection primarily affecting the central nervous system and usually transmitted by animal bites or scratches. After an incubation period usually lasting between 1 and 3 months but which can extend up to 1 year, about 80% of individuals infected with rabies present with the classic furious rabies characterized by hyperactivity, excitable behaviour, hallucinations, lack of coordination, hydrophobia and aerophobia. In 20% of remaining cases, individuals present paralytic rabies that typically starts at the site of the bite and gradually spreads to other parts of the body. It is associated with progressive lower motor neuron weakness. These paralytic forms are underreported.

Once symptoms have appeared, death is nearly always inevitable. According to the WHO, rabies is currently responsible for 59,000 human deaths per year, mainly reported in Africa and Asia. It remains a threat under-appreciated by healthcare practitioners in many endemic areas, often owing to lack of rapid diagnostic tools, postmortem evaluation, and public health reporting.

According to the CDC, exposure to rabid dogs is still the cause of over 90% of human exposures to rabies and of more than 95% of human rabies deaths worldwide.

## Available therapies and unmet medical need

There is no treatment for rabies. Once the symptoms have begun, the disease is almost always fatal. However, human death from rabies can be effectively prevented through vaccination, by rabies vaccine PrEP in individuals with high risk of exposure, and as part of PEP when administered immediately after suspect rabies exposure. The objective of PEP is to remove free virus from tissues by both washing the wounds, neutralizing the rabies virus via passive immunization (rabies immunoglobulin, RIG) in previously non-immunized individuals, and inducing a rabies virus-specific immune response through vaccination before rabies virus can replicate in the central nervous system (Plotkin SA., Clin Infect Dis., 2000). Although PrEP does not eliminate the need of PEP in case of rabies exposure, it simplifies the rabies PEP schedule since a reduced number of vaccine doses is needed and RIG is not required (Rao AK et al., Morb Mortal Wkly Rep., 2022).

Several rabies vaccines containing inactivated rabies virus, intended for both PrEP and PEP in all age groups, are available in European countries. These include Verorab (Vero cell based, first licensed in 1985 in France) licensed by Sanofi, and, additionally, Rabipur (chick embryo cell based, current MAH: Bavarian Nordic A/S).

## Vaccination regimens

There are various PrEP and PEP vaccination schedules depending on the WHO recommendations and official recommendations worldwide. VRVg is intended to cover most of these vaccination schedules. It is to be noted that the paediatric population is to receive the same vaccination regimens (number of vaccine doses) and dosage as adults. This is in line with all available marketed rabies vaccines and recommendations worldwide, which provide a single dosage applicable to the entire population, avoiding complexity in rabies vaccination management policies and optimal use of vaccine supply.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 2.2. Aspects of development

The purpose of VaxRabeo is to ultimately replace both Sanofi rabies vaccines, Imovax Rabies, and Verorab, across the globe with the same indication (i.e., PrEP and PEP for rabies in all age groups).

VRVg development was adapted over time to various regulatory, pharmaceutical, and/or clinical constraints and was therefore conducted through stepwise process evolutions named VRVg-1 and VRVg-2 (VaxRabeo), respectively.

Figure 1: Overview of VRVg clinical development

<!-- image -->

During the first part of the clinical development plan (CDP) wherein VRVg-1 was tested in overall five clinical studies with either Verorab or Imovax Rabies as comparators, results from two clinical studies, both conducted in the US with Imovax Rabies as a comparator (i.e., studies VRV02 and VRV04), showed unexpectedly low immunogenicity of VRVg-1.

Therefore, the decision was made to modify the VRVg-1 formulation to ensure an enhanced immune response leading to the development of VRVg-2 Step 1, hereafter referred as VRVg-2. Of note, \"VRVg-1 Step 1\" was only used as an active comparator in a Phase 2 study (VRV11) conducted in the US; the purpose of this study was to investigate the antigen dose response of the VRVg-2 formulation, and to select the appropriate antigen dosage that induces the expected robust immune response with an adequate safety profile.

Although the main product attributes of VRVg-2 remain similar to VRVg-1, VRVg-2 differentiates from VRVg-1 through a higher antigen content as well as the addition of a highly purified rHA as a stabilising excipient.

Overall, 4 Phase 3 studies were conducted with VRVg-2 (VRV09, VRV12, VRV13, and VRV00014). Among these 4 studies, 2 pivotal Phase 3 studies were carried out to demonstrate the non-inferiority of VRVg-2 versus Verorab and Imovax Rabies through PrEP vaccination regimen (VRV12) and through PEP vaccination regimen (VRV13):

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- VRV12 was conducted both in a paediatric population aged ≥ 1 to &lt; 18 years and adults aged ≥ 18 years and aimed to assess the PrEP intramuscular (IM) 2-dose and 3-dose vaccination regimens. A booster dose was also documented in this study.
- VRV13 was conducted in adults aged ≥ 18 years and aimed to assess the same PEP IM 4- and 5-dose Essen regimen as in VRV11.

Two other Phase 3 descriptive studies were carried out to document additional PEP regimens:

- VRV00014 was conducted in adults aged ≥ 18 years to assess the PEP IM Zagreb regimen.
- VRV09 was conducted in paediatric population aged ≥ 1 to &lt; 18 years and adults aged ≥ 18 years to assess the PEP intradermal (ID) Thai Red Cross (TRC) regimen and the PEP ID Institut Pasteur du Cambodge (IPC) regimen.

## 2.3. Description of the product

The Sanofi rabies vaccine Drug Substance (DS) is an inactivated rabies virus derived from Wistar Rabies Strain Pitman Moore/WI38 1503-3M produced on Vero cells, without raw materials from human or animal origin used in routine production, which is purified and then inactivated with betapropiolactone. The DS is highly purified and presents a very low Vero host cell residual DNA content (≤ 100 picograms per dose).

The VRVg Drug Product (DP) is a purified, inactivated, and freeze-dried rabies vaccine formulated with a stabilizer without preservative. It is a white homogeneous cake, supplied in vials. The DP is a sterile freeze-dried form to be stored at +5°C ± 3°C.

The freeze-dried VRVg DP, present in the vial, is to be reconstituted with 0.5 mL of solvent (sodium chloride solution [NaCl] 0.4%), i.e., the full content of the pre-filled syringe. After reconstitution, the product is a clear to opalescent colourless liquid and contains at least 6.8 IU inactivated rabies virus.

One IM dose consists of 0.5 mL of reconstituted vaccine (entire content of the vial) and one ID dose consists of 0.1 mL of reconstituted vaccine.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The vaccine induces production of rabies virus-neutralising antibodies (RVNA). A threshold of RVNA titre of at least 0.5 IU/mL is considered as an adequate immune response after vaccination, as per WHO recommendation. Rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies are directed against the surface G glycoprotein. They exert their protective function by blocking domains of the viral glycoprotein surface required for the attachment of the virus to susceptible cells.

The product has not yet been approved in any market.

The proposed indication is for pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis against rabies in individuals of all age groups.

VRVg belongs to the anti-infective for systemic use pharmacological class - Vaccines group anatomical therapeutic chemical (ATC) code: J07BG01.

## 2.4. Inspection issues

## 2.4.1. Good manufacturing practice (GMP) inspections

The GMP certificate for the SWI - Neuville-sur-Saône (NVL) site reflects QC testing but not drug substance manufacturing activities. ANSM (the supervisory authority) stated that the site can be considered satisfactory for drug substance manufacture.

All other sites are GMP compliant and have valid GMP certificates.

No inspection required.

## 2.4.2. Good laboratory practice (GLP) inspections

The repeat dose toxicity study VRG.RDrb08 and the DART study VRG.DVrb08/12 were performed in the same site. The facility was inspected in October 2007 and in October 2009 and the studies were performed in 2008 with a final study report completed in October 2009. For the repeat dose toxicity study for VRVg-2, the site was inspected in January 2016, 2017 and 2018 and the final study report was completed in January 2017.

For all the toxicity studies performed by the applicant, sites were indeed considered GLP compliant at study time. All relevant toxicological studies were thus conducted according to GLP, except the immunogenicity study phase of the studies conducted with VRVg-1 (repeated dose toxicity and the DART studies) which were conducted in a non-GLP facility. The absence of GLP compliance for the immunogenicity study phases was considered not to have adversely affected the outcome or interpretation of the study results. This phase was conducted at internal test site, which was considered to have the most appropriate scientific expertise on parameters not used as direct safety endpoints. The vaccines used in the GLP nonclinical safety studies were manufactured according to current GMP.

In conclusion, there is no issue with the GLP status of the toxicity studies performed by the applicant.

No inspection required.

## 2.4.3. Good clinical practice (GCP) inspections

A request for GCP inspection has been adopted for the following clinical study: VRV12.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The pertinent report of the routine GCP inspection concluded that despite the observed areas of ICHGCP non-compliance and the need for CAPAs to be implemented for the findings observed, the data reported for clinical trial VRV12 are still considered to be of sufficient integrity and quality to be used.

## 3. Quality aspects

## 3.1. Introduction

The finished product (FP) is presented as powder and solvent for suspension for injection containing ≥6.8 International Units (nominal content: 9 IU/vial) of inactivated Rabies virus (Wistar Rabies strain PM/WI38 1503-3M produced on Vero cells) as active substance (AS), formulated with a stabiliser and recombinant human albumin (rHA).

The finished product is supplied in packs of 1 or 10 co-packaged powder vials and solvent pre-filled syringes (PFSs) as follows:

Freeze-dried powder in a glass vial contains:

- Inactivated Rabies virus (Wistar Rabies strain PM/WI38 1503-3M produced on Vero cells)
- Recombinant human albumin (rHA)
- Essential amino acids (L-cystine, L-tyrosine, L-arginine HCl, L-histidine, L-isoleucine, L-leucine, L-lysine HCl, L-methionine, L-phenylalanine, L-threonine, L-tryptophan, and L-valine)
- Non-essential amino acids (L-alanine, L-asparagine, L-aspartic acid, L-glutamic acid, L-proline, L-serine and glycine),
- Maltose monohydrate,
- Sorbitol,
- Mineral salts (sodium dihydrogen phosphate dihydrate, disodium phosphate dihydrate),
- Urea,
- Sodium glutamate monohydrate,
- Disodium edetate (EDTA),
- Poloxamer P188,
- Hydrochloric acid (HCl)*,
- Sodium hydroxide (NaOH)*.

*Also used for pH adjustment

Solvent in a glass PFS with luer lock vial adaptor contains:

- Sodium chloride (NaCl) (0.4%)
- Water for injections

Two separate needles for reconstitution and administration are co-packaged in the pack size of 1 vial and 1 pre-filled syringe.

## 3.2. Active substance

## 3.2.1. General information

VaxRabeo is a rabies vaccine containing the beta-propiolactone-inactivated rabies virus (Wistar rabies strain PM/WI38 1503-3M produced on Vero cells) as the active substance (common name: rabies vaccine (inactivated) for human use). The rabies virus belongs to the family of Rhabdoviridae with an unsegmented linear negative RNA genome of about 12 kb, encoding five viral proteins: nucleoprotein (N protein), phosphoprotein (P protein), matrix (M) protein, glycoprotein (G protein), and large (L) polymerase protein. The rabies virus is an enveloped virus, it has a bullet-like shape with a length of about 180 nm and a cross-sectional diameter of about 80 nm. Virus structure and the structure of the main target for neutralising antibodies (G protein, the only envelope protein) including the major antigenic sites (i.e. site II grouping residues 34 to 42 and 198 to 200, in close proximity due to the presence of a disulfide bond between cysteine residues 35 and 207 and site III corresponding to residues 330 to 338) are described in the dossier. From all the rabies viral proteins, the G protein is the only antigen capable of inducing specific neutralising antibodies. The presence of the transmembrane domain is critical to several functions: to stabilise the native conformation of the overall molecule, for receptor recognition and for induction of neutralising antibodies. The amino acid sequence of protein G has been provided with peptide signal, the transmembrane and the three potential glycosylation sites being outlined.

## 3.2.2. Manufacture, process controls and process development

## Description of manufacturing process and process controls

The active substance is manufactured at Sanofi Winthrop Industrie, 31-33 Quai Armand Barbès, 69250 Neuville-sur-Saône, France.

Evidence of good manufacturing practice (GMP) compliance has been presented for all manufacturing sites. The manufacturing and import authorization (MIA) and GMP certificate provided for SWI - Neuville-sur-Saône (NVL) site does not cover manufacture and storage of active substance (manufacturing activities listed are restricted to batch certification and QC testing). However, the additional evidence provided by the supervisory authority and QP declaration is sufficient to confirm GMP compliance.

The VRVg (company internal name: purified Vero rabies vaccine global- serum free) active substance manufacturing process is described in sufficient detail. The major manufacturing process steps of the active substance include: Vero cell culture, viral culture and clarification, purification, inactivation using beta-propiolactone (BPL), ultracentrifugation, concentration and stabilization. Upstream processing starts with amplification of Vero cells obtained from the working cell bank (WCB). Following amplification steps, cells are infected with the working seed lot. Commercial scale size is defined. Upstream and downstream processing including inactivation using beta-propiolactone (BPL) are suitably described.

The inactivated purified harvest may be stored in sterile storage bags after 0.2 µm filtration. The manufacturing flow is provided in the dossier.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Critical in-process control tests are applied at relevant manufacturing steps with acceptable limits, including, absence of residual infectious virus and residual DNA content with appropriate acceptance criteria. No reprocessing is claimed and hence not allowed. One active substance batch is defined as the purified and inactivated pool of a specified number of individual harvests from one viral seed lot inoculation. The final active substance volume per batch is given in the dossier.

Process hold times are proposed for specified intermediates and sufficiently justified based on process validation studies.

## Control of materials

## Raw materials

Adequate information on raw materials used in the active substance manufacturing process has been submitted. Compendial raw materials are tested in accordance with the corresponding monograph, while specifications (including analytical procedures) for non-compendial raw materials are presented. Information on qualitative composition of proprietary media has been provided, the risk arising from residual media components can be considered as negligible. No human or animal derived materials are used in the active substance manufacturing process and acceptable documents have been provided for raw materials of biological origin used in the establishment of Vero cell substrate and viral seed lots.

## Cell Banks

A two-tiered cell banking system is used and sufficient information is provided regarding testing of master cell bank (MCB) and working cell banks (WCBs). The animal free WCBs used for the production of the VRVg active substance are established at the same passage level as the current banks used for the production of other licensed Sanofi vaccines. Cell banks were principally tested in compliance with Ph. Eur. 5.2.3, ICHQ5A and ICHQ5D requirements. Methods used for cell bank characterisation testing were shown to be suitable for their intended purpose. The MCB was tested for microbial contaminants, adventitious agents , and identity. WCBs at specific passages were evaluated for identity, microbial contaminants, adventitious agents and tumorigenicity. The initial cell bank characterisation testing was later complemented by bacterial and fungal sterility test on vials, and additional tests for adventitious agents. Testing was mainly performed on WCB vials to secure MCB stockpile, this can be accepted. The maximum number of passages allowed during routine production is defined. Stability of cell banks was confirmed for the WCBs, respective data are available in the dossier. The stability of MCB is demonstrated during the manufacture of a new WCB. The latest MCB stability data will be provided

when a new WCB is manufactured (Recommendation 1).

## Viral seed lots

The VRVg virus seed lots are derived from the Pitman Moore (PM) rabies viral strain that is currently used as well in the production of other licensed Sanofi rabies vaccines. The history of the strain is described in sufficient detail. The existing master virus seed Lot (MSL) produced in 1972 is used for manufacturing of Sanofi's currently approved vaccines. A serum free intermediate seed lot (ISL) was produced before the establishment of new serum working seed lots (WSL) to secure supply. The serum free ISL and WSL were tested in line with Ph. Eur. 0216 and Ph. Eur. 2.6.16 for identity, virus concentration, and extraneous agents. The WSL was additionally tested for mycobacteria, for extraneous agents to confirm absence of retroviruses. ISL and WSL complied with acceptance criteria. Suitability of respective methods has been demonstrated. Considering implementation of a new version of Ph. Eur. 2.6.16, the VRVg WSL was additionally tested for absence of Spiroplasma by culture method, detection of adventitious virus, and tested for extraneous agents using Cells (MRC-5 and Vero Cells). Compendial methods were verified and validation data demonstrating suitability of the method have been provided. Stability data demonstrating that the WSL remains stable over 120 months when stored at ≤ -70°C have been provided. Genetic stability of G protein is addressed in the characterisation section (see below). No protocol for release of future WCBs/WSLs has been provided.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Control of critical steps and intermediates

Critical process parameters (CPPs) and critical, in-process control tests (IPCTs) are tabulated in the dossier. For classification of process parameters, a risk assessment was performed with a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) (FMEA) approach. A major objection (MO) was raised on the control strategy. Process characterisation data supporting the proposed acceptance criteria/limits for critical process parameters and justification for non-critical PP assignment were missing. Sufficient details on the process criticality analysis methodology and process parameter categorisation as well as a detailed risk ranking score for each process parameter analysed have now been provided. The classification of process parameters as either CPP or non key process parameters (nKPP) is considered sufficiently justified. Acceptance criteria/limits for CPPs are sufficiently justified based on supportive studies carried out either at industrial scale, at lab-scale or through design of experiments. Proposed limits for IPCTs are acceptable. The MO has been resolved. There are no intermediates in the VRVg active substance manufacturing process.

## Process validation

The active substance manufacturing process has been validated adequately. Consistency in production has been shown on a suitable number of full-scale commercial batches manufactured at set point conditions. All acceptance criteria for the critical operational parameters and likewise acceptance criteria for the in-process tests are fulfilled demonstrating that the process consistently produces active substance of reproducible quality that complies with the predetermined specification and in-process acceptance criteria. The reproducibility of the inactivation step was validated through the production of a suitable number of consecutive batches. All CPP, IPCT comply with their acceptance criteria. The inactivation kinetics profile was comparable between the batches. Process holding times during the manufacture of the VRVg active substance have been defined. The proposed hold times are sufficiently supported by process validation data. At scale lifetime validation studies on the purification systems were conducted at the Marcy l'Etoile (MLE) manufacturing site. The study principally justifies the proposed lifetime for the purification systems, however, has some limitations which will be addressed during validation at the NVL site. A protocol for validation of the purification systems at the NVL site has been provided. The applicant has committed to provide purification system lifetime validation data for the NVL site once available (Recommendation 2).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Manufacturing process development

VRVg active substance manufacturing was initially conducted at a smaller scale than commercial production. Compared to the manufacturing process of Verorab (currently marketed within several member states within the EU), process improvements were introduced including removal of components derived from human or animal origin, removal of antibiotics from WSL and AS production, decrease of the final residual DNA content and downstream process improvements. The process was further modified (process version 'VRVg optimised') to optimize the equipment media and upstream/downstream process steps. To increase the production capacity, the viral culture was scaledup at the MLE site. Concomitant changes included scale-up of the WSL, filtration changes and changes for the simplification of the purification process. For commercialisation, the VRVg step 1 process has been transferred from the MLE site to the NVL site (VRVg step 2). Process changes include site-specific adaptions (i.e. automation of processes, industrial adaptations including equipment design) and change of the container closure system.

## Comparability

Comparability studies were performed to support pharmaceutical development (See Section 2.2 Aspects of Development). A comparability exercise has been conducted to support the transfer of the Verorab label claims to VRVg vaccine. Commercial Verorab batches were compared to VRVg step 1 batches. For the tested attributes no obvious differences between both products were observed. Justification for not performing extensive comparability testing as originally proposed in the scientific advice have been provided. Based on the data provided it can be concluded that active substances from both products are sufficiently recognised thereby confirming presence of relevant epitopes and antigenicity. Comparability of active substance stability was demonstrated. The comparability data do not indicate significant differences in quality of active substance between Verorab and VaxRabeo. A comparability exercise was performed to demonstrate comparability of VRVg step 1 material manufactured at the MLE site to VRVg step 2 manufactured at the NVL site. The comparability exercise was comprised of relevant release, stability and characterisation tests. Tests and analytical methods to assess product quality attributes (PQA) with their associated comparability acceptance criteria are outlined. For the tested attributes no significant differences between VRVg step 1 and VRVg step 2 AS were observed. Nevertheless, it is agreed that these differences (if any) are not expected to impact downstream performance.

## Critical Quality Attributes and Process Criticality Analysis

Critical quality attributes (CQAs), non-CQA and key performance attributes (KPA) were identified and linked to process parameters or material attributes. CQAs were defined based on impact on safety and efficacy. The list of CQAs and KPAs is considered appropriate for the type of product and the analytical testing strategy appears suitable to ensure adequate quality. CPPs were defined following process criticality analysis (PCA) using a standard FMEA approach and considering prior knowledge acquired through the VRVg active substance manufacturing development at the MLE site. Risk ranking scores have been provided for each process parameter analysis and definition of CPPs is sufficiently justified. Process characterisation studies supporting the proposed acceptance criteria/limits for CPPs have been provided. In-process control tests are performed at relevant manufacturing steps (see section on control of

critical steps and intermediates).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Transport qualification

Transport of the active substance from NVL to the finished product manufacturing site Val-de-Reuil (VDR) can be considered as sufficiently qualified.

## Extractables and Leachables Risk Assessment

A risk assessment related to extractables and leachables was conducted for all product contact materials. \"Medium Risk\" contact materials were identified and evaluated in an extractables study. A commitment to providing results for the ongoing extractable study performed for the flask used for storage and transfer of solutions has been provided (Recommendation 3).

## 3.2.3. Characterisation and impurities

Characterisation studies were performed on a suitable number of process validation batches manufactured at the commercial site. Particle size distribution and viral morphology were comparable for the batches analysed. Protein profiling identified the five viral rabies proteins. Lipid composition analysis revealed cholesterol as the major lipid, phospholipids are also largely present. Triglycerides and ceramides are minor components. Analysis has confirmed the same viral particle conformation for all batches. Genetic stability of G protein was analysed. Based on bioinformatics analysis, no impact on antigen recognition, viral neutralisation, or on binding with the cellular receptor of the virus is foreseen. Three potential glycosylation sites are contained within the G protein sequence. N-glycan analysis showed a similar glycan profile with predominance of neutral hybrids/complex charged N-glycans.

Product-related impurities were analysed. Presence and intactness of viral proteins and absence of aggregates have been confirmed. Residual host-cell proteins, residual host-cell DNA, residual BPL are indicated as process-related impurities and are adequately controlled. Residual levels of other specified process-related impurities are also suitably discussed.

## 3.2.4. Control of active substance

## Specifications

The active substance release and shelf-life specifications are described in the dossier. The test methods include appropriate physico-chemical methods and methods for identity, purity, potency and safety. An MO was raised on the specifications, and subsequently, the list of active substance release specifications was expanded to include further tests (MO resolved).

## Analytical procedures and reference standards

References to relevant Ph. Eur. chapters have been provided for the compendial methods. High level analytical method descriptions have been provided for in-house methods. Testing for effective inactivation is performed in line with the requirements stated in Ph. Eur. 0216.

Method validation reports were not provided for compendial methods, which is principally acceptable. Verification data for the bacterial and fungal contamination test method (Ph. Eur. 2.6.1) have been provided and confirm method suitability. The rabies virus concentration and identity test and the test for control of effective inactivation are sufficiently validated in line with ICH Q2 and considered suitable for their intended purpose.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The reference material used to quantify G protein content at active substance level is the same as used for finished product testing, a cross-reference has been included in the dossier.

The quantification of G protein is assessed by a double-sandwich ELISA method according to Ph. Eur. monograph 0216 using two specific monoclonal antibodies. The G protein content of the product is determined in IU/mL using an internal reference standard calibrated against the 7 th WHO International Standard for Rabies vaccine.

## Batch analysis

Batch analysis data for the process validation batches of the active substance are provided. Additional batch data including clinical batches are presented in dossier section S.2.6.

The results are within the specifications and confirm consistency of the manufacturing process.

## 3.2.5. Stability

Stability studies were performed considering ICH Q5C and ICH Q1A guidelines.

The commercial active substance is stored in sterile single use bag systems . The film in contact with the product is different depending on the suppliers used. The bags are received ready-to-use after sterilisation from the suppliers. Confirmation that the single use bags comply with international standards including qualification in line with Ph. Eur. 3.2.2.1 has been provided. Supplier certificates have been included in the dossier.

The shelf life was confirmed with stability data from AS batches manufactured at MLE and NVL. Studied parameters are described in the dossier. The test methods include appropriate physicochemical methods and methods for potency and safety. The data confirmed the proposed shelf life and storage conditions for AS.

## 3.3. Finished medicinal product - Freeze-dried powder

## 3.3.1. Description of the product and pharmaceutical development

## Description of the product

The VRVg FP is a sterile, freeze-dried powder for intramuscular (IM) or intradermal injection (ID) upon reconstitution with 0.5 mL sterile solvent. It is supplied in a Type I glass vial with a chlorobutyl or bromobutyl stopper and a flip-off aluminium/polypropylene cap.

One vial contains at least 6.8 International Units (nominal content: 9 IU/vial) of inactivated Rabies virus (Wistar Rabies strain PM/WI38 1503-3M produced on Vero cells) as active substance. One intramuscular dose consists of the entire contents of the reconstituted vaccine (i.e., 0.5 mL), one intradermal dose consists of 0.1 mL of the reconstituted vaccine (i.e., up to five doses per vial). The composition of the finished product is shown in Table 2.

The vaccine is formulated with a stabilising solution (see Table 3), recombinant human albumin (rHA), and without preservative. Many of the components of the stabilising solution are well known pharmaceutical ingredients and their quality is compliant with Ph. Eur. standards. The choice of excipients has been justified satisfactorily. Non-compendial excipients are controlled to in-house specifications.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The freeze-dried powder forms a white homogeneous cake. After reconstitution, the product is a clear to opalescent colourless liquid.

The solvent for reconstitution (0.4% sodium chloride solution) is provided in a co-packaged PFS with fitted luer-lock adapter (please refer to the separate FP section). Two separate CE-marked needles for reconstitution and administration may be co-packaged.

## Pharmaceutical development

The aim of the pharmaceutical development was to develop a purified, inactivated and freeze-dried rabies vaccine for intramuscular and intradermal administration that is manufactured without raw materials of animal or human origin. The VRVg rabies vaccine is intended to replace, worldwide, the currently authorised Verorab and Imovax rabies vaccines. The excipients were selected to stabilise the active substance (stabilising solution). The formulation provides for a physiologic pH and isotonicity of the reconstituted vaccine. Compatibility of VRVg with the excipients was studied during formulation development and is demonstrated by the available long-term stability data. Three formulations, i.e., VRVg-1, VRVg-2 step 1, and VRVg-2 step 2, were used during development of VRVg. Whereas presentation and solvent remained unchanged throughout development, the formulation and antigen target concentration of VRVg was changed throughout clinical development. Initially a vaccine with a lower antigen formulation target (and without rHA was used (VRVg-1). For studies VRV11 (Phase 2), VRV09, VRV12, VRV13, and VRV014 (all Phase 3), the antigen target concentration was raised and rHA was added to stabilise. For discussion of comparability please refer to the manufacturing process development section below. The proposed specifications for the non-compendial excipients maltose monohydrate and sodium hydroxide 10 N as well as for the non-compendial essential/non-essential amino acids are deemed acceptable; the individual amino acids comply with the corresponding Ph. Eur. monographs. The inhouse specifications for the non-compendial rHA are deemed sufficient; an agreement is in place with the supplier of this excipient to notify the MAH in case of changes to the specifications in force at the supplier (as documented in section A.3). Compendial methods are used for control of both, compendial and non-compendial excipients. The stabilising solution is a multi-component stabiliser. Of note, comparable multi-component stabilisers are also used for other authorised vaccines marketed by Sanofi including Verorab. No excipients of animal or human origin are used. There is no novel excipient used in the finished product formulation. As discussed in EMA-SA Case No. EMA/SA/0000152169, rHA has previously been approved in EU as a constituent in COVID-19 Vaccine Valneva (inactivated, adjuvanted) and hence, is no longer considered as a novel excipient for the intramuscular or intradermal administration route. As recombinant human albumin (rHA) is a complex biological excipient, detailed information has been included in section A.3. The rHA is produced in yeast cells. Sufficiently detailed information has been provided on the manufacturers, manufacturing process, control of materials, process validation, impurities, and adventitious agents. In depth characterisation of rHA was performed as well as comparison with plasma-derived human albumin. It was shown that rHA is identical to human albumin and shows even higher purity than plasma-derived albumin. The specifications and analytical methods for release of rHA are deemed acceptable. Batch release data are provided for several batches showing that Quality Control (QC) test results are very consistent and comply with the specifications. Details are provided on the container closure, a glass vial with bromobutyl stopper (materials are compliant with respective Ph. Eur. monographs) and a flip-off cap. Stability data support the proposed shelf-life of rHA of 60 months when stored at 2-8°C. At 25°C the rHA remains stable for 36 months.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The data provided for the rHA excipient are deemed sufficient and acceptable.

## Manufacturing process development

Process development and control strategy Based on the quality target product profile the relevant CQAs have been identified and rationale for their classification as CQA have been provided. For each identified CQA, a release test/ specification test, IPCT, or characterisation test has been established. The analytical control strategy appears adequate and in line with regulatory expectations. Overall, the changes in analytical methods and in release and shelf-life specifications for excipients, final bulk product (FBP), and freeze-dried FP implemented during development are sufficiently described and justified. The manufacturing process for VRVg was developed based on the manufacturing process for Verorab. Three different FP manufacturing process versions were used throughout development, i.e. VRVg-1 used for earlier clinical studies (low relevance for the current procedure), VRVg-2 step 1 used to manufacture vaccine for the relevant Phase 2 and 3 studies, and the intended commercial FP manufacturing process VRVg-2 step 2. The genealogy of the relevant VRVg FP lots manufactured throughout development and corresponding batch release data are presented in the dossier. The process changes implemented during development of the FP process were mainly related to changes of manufacturing facility and scale, use of AS from different AS manufacturing processes (i.e. VRVg step 1 vs. VRVg step 2), changes in formulation, and optimisation of the process. Except the use of VRVg-2 instead of VRVg-1 AS, all these changes were implemented during development of VRVg-1 (i.e. prior to manufacture of VRVg-2 step 1 FP used for the relevant clinical studies VRV11, VRV09, VRV12, VRV13, and VRV014). For commercial manufacture, the VRVg-2 step 1 process was transferred from Sanofi Marcy l´Etoile (MLE) to Sanofi Val de Reuil (VDR) and changes included upscaling, resulting in the process called VRVg-2 step 2. The presented process development studies address thawing of active substance (freeze/thaw, hold time), homogeneity of the FBP (mixing study, sedimentation), potential product degradation by mixing, sterilising filtration prior to filling (filter validation including compatibility, extractables studies, particle release, and bacterial retention studies), as well as robustness of the lyophilisation process. Additional aspects (e.g. hold times, product adsorption to filter) were evaluated during process validation. Critical process parameters (CPPs), KPPs, and nKPPs have been identified based on a process criticality analysis and process development studies. The ranges for the CPPs are adequately supported by development studies and process validation. Comparability Two analytical comparability exercises were performed at FP level. One comparability exercise compared Verorab and VRVg-2 step 1 to support the transfer of the Verorab label claims to the VRVg vaccine. In another comparability exercise, FP manufactured according to process VRVg-2 step 1 or process VRVg-2 step 2 was compared to demonstrate that the process transfer and associated changes implemented at the intended commercial site had no impact on product quality, and thus, on safety and efficacy. Both comparability exercises were subject to EMA scientific advice. Relevant FP quality attributes were evaluated using release, stability, and additional characterisation methods. However, it should be noted that due to the type of product, the low active substance concentration in FP, and the presence of recombinant human albumin the analytical accessibility is limited at FP stage. Commercial Verorab lots were compared to lots manufactured according to process VRVg-2 step 1. For most parameters, comparability was evaluated against the release and stability specification limits of the respective product which is insufficient to conclude on comparability. No justification is given for any of the comparability acceptance criteria. However, as individual analytical results are provided and allow an independent assessment of comparability, this issue is not pursued. Lots manufactured according to process VRVg-2 step 1 were compared to process validation lots manufactured using process VRVg-2 step 2. The stability profile appears to be comparable between both products. No relevant differences are noted for any of the tested parameters including G protein content and particle size profile. Under provision of the study limitations (small number of lots, all VRVg-2 Step 1 FP lots originate from the same AS batch, poor analytical accessibility of FP), it is agreed that VRVg-2 step 1 FP and VRVg-2 step 2 FP appear analytically comparable. The observed minor differences are not expected to negatively impact clinical performance of the vaccine. Please also refer to the discussion of comparability between the respective AS processes VRVg step 1 and VRVg step 2. FP shipping FP is shipped at 5 ± 3°C by sea, by air and by road transport. The presented transportation simulation studies and shipping studies demonstrate that the shipping process for FP is under control and maintains refrigerated conditions during transportation. Container closure Final bulk product is stored in stainless steel tanks. The container closure system (CCS) for FP is a Type I borosilicate glass vial closed with a lubricated halobutyl rubber stopper commonly used for parenteral products including other authorised Sanofi products. The components comply with compendial requirements (i.e., Ph. Eur. 3.2.1, 3.2.9 respectively). The chosen CCS was shown to be suitable in terms of compatibility, container closure integrity, and safety. The VRVg vaccine does not contain any preservative. Sterility is sufficiently ensured by complementary measures taken (e.g. bioburden reduction filtration and sterilising filtration followed by aseptic filling, IPC and release testing for microbiological contaminants). Compatibility of the freeze-dried product (VRVg-2 Step 1 and VRVg-2 step 2) with the 0.4% NaCl solvent has been demonstrated by stability and in-use studies performed with reconstituted vaccine. The handling instructions described in the product information are supported by these studies.

## 3.3.2. Manufacture of the product and process controls

Manufacturing process and controls The name, address and responsibility of each manufacturer involved in finished product manufacture and testing is described in the dossier. The manufacturer responsible for batch release is Sanofi Winthrop Industrie (Sanofi) -Val de Reuil (VDR) site, Parc Industriel d'Incarville, Voie De L'Institut, P.O. Box 101, 27100 Val de Reuil, France. Valid MIAs and GMP certificates covering the performed activities at all sites are available.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The manufacturing process is based on common pharmaceutical processing steps and includes the following steps: preparation of the excipients (rHA solution, stabiliser solution), AS thawing, final bulk product (FBP) production including formulation and bioburden reduction filtration, preparation of the container closure system, on-line sterilising filtration of FBP, aseptic filling of FBP, freeze-drying and stoppering, capping, 100% verification of container closure integrity, 100% visual inspection, and secondary packaging and labelling. The freeze-dried FP is labelled and co-packaged with PFS with solvent (2 needles are provided in the pack size of 1 vial and 1 pre-filled syringe), and the finished product is finally stored +5°C ± 3°C.

The target batch size of FBP and expected number of vials of freeze-dried product are described in the dossier.

Different batches of inactivated viral rabies bulk may be pooled for manufacture of FP.

Reprocessing is not described and hence, not allowed.

The process description is generally in line with the requirements of the Guideline on manufacture of the finished dosage form EMA/CHMP/QWP/245074/2015. The date of the start of the filling is defined as the date of manufacture of the freeze-dried FP which is acceptable.

The identified CPPs are consistent with regulatory expectations, and the proposed parameters ranges are supported by development or validation data.

The in-process controls meet regulatory expectations for this type of process and appear adequate to ensure consistent quality of FP as part of the overall control strategy.

All hold times are justified by hold time and stability studies.

The glass vials and the stoppers are sterilised by dry heat treatment or steam sterilisation, respectively, in accordance with Ph. Eur. requirements.

## Process validation

The Process performance qualification (PPQ) encompassed manufacture of a suitable number of consecutive FBP batches and freeze-dried FP lots at commercial scale at the intended commercial site VDR according to the proposed commercial manufacturing process VRVg-2 step 2 using target conditions at target scale. The PPQ batches were manufactured using the VRVg-2 step 2 AS PPQ batches.

All CPPs as well as all IPC and release tests comply with their acceptance criteria. The results of the integrity check and the visual inspection meet the defined limits. Results are consistent across the FBP batches/FP lots. No relevant product adsorption to the bioburden reduction filter or the sterilising filter was observed. Consistency of filling as well as consistent product quality throughout filling and within the freeze-dryer has been sufficiently demonstrated.

Results for initial and annual re-validation media fill runs comply with their acceptance criteria and support the aseptic filling duration.

Overall, the PPQ results in combination with development data presented in 3.2.P.2.3 and the results from media fills demonstrate that the proposed commercial FP manufacturing process is capable of delivering FP of consistent and acceptable quality.

## 3.3.3. Control of Finished Product

## Specifications

Final bulk product The FBP release and shelf-life specifications are described in the dossier. The test methods include appropriate methods for potency and safety at the appropriate stage. Finished product The proposed set of attributes tested at FP are described in the dossier. The test methods include appropriate physico-chemical methods and methods for identity, purity, potency and safety. The end of shelf life (EOSL) specification is described in the dossier. The test methods include appropriate physico-chemical and potency methods. The Applicant´s approach to remove specific physico-chemical, identity, purity, and safety tests from the EOSL specification is acceptable. The levels of elemental impurities detected in the leachables study performed on FP in the commercial CCS do not give raise to concerns. A risk assessment and a control strategy for elemental impurities in accordance with ICH Q3D has been provided. A risk assessment concerning the potential presence of nitrosamine impurities in the finished product was performed according to the applicable guidance. Based on the information provided, there is no risk of nitrosamine impurities in the finished product. Therefore, no specific control measures are

deemed necessary.

## Analytical procedures and reference standards

## Analytical procedures

References to relevant Ph. Eur. chapters have been provided for the compendial methods. Acceptable method descriptions are available for in-house methods. As discussed in a preceding EMA-SA, the Applicant proposes to replace the in vivo NIH potency assay by the G protein ELISA. Principally, replacement of the in vivo potency assay by an immunochemical assay is in line with Ph. Eur. 0216 and strongly endorsed under consideration of the 3Rs. The G protein sandwich ELISA is based on quantitation of native rabies G protein by two neutralising monoclonal antibodies (mAb clone 1112-1 for capture and mAb clone D1-25 for detection) recognising antigenic site III or antigenic site II (conformational epitope) of the G protein. The relevant method performance characteristics specificity, dilutional linearity, accuracy, and precision (repeatability, intermediate precision) have been validated in accordance with ICH Q2 and demonstrate that the method is suitable for quantitation and identification of G protein in FP samples. Referenced publications of Sanofi-Pasteur (Chabaud-Riou et al., 2017, Biologicals 46: 124-129, Toinon et al., 2019) and results from a collaborative international study (Morgeaux et al, 2017, Vaccine 35: 966 - 971) indicate that ELISA systems based on the two mAbs are stability-indicating and show agreement with potency data determined by the in vivo NIH assay. Concerning the correlation between the G protein ELISA and the in vivo NIH assay it is acknowledged that demonstration of a strict correlation between both assays is difficult due to the high variability of the in vivo assay. Nevertheless, a general agreement between both methods is evident from the published data and the results presented in the dossier. The relevant data (i.e. demonstration of stability-indicating capability, agreement between in vivo NIH assay and ELISA) from the publications have been filed in the dossier.

In summary, the G protein ELISA was demonstrated to be a suitable potency assay. Compared to the NIH in vivo assay, the G protein ELISA is more precise, and the results show a better correlation to immunogenicity.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Method validation reports were not provided for compendial methods, which is principally acceptable. Acceptable method validation summaries are provided for applicable methods, demonstrating the methods are suitable for the intended use for methods compliant with compendial monographs (which provide a general description of the methods).

## Reference materials

The G protein content of AS, FBP, and FP samples is determined against a product-specific Reference Standard that has been calibrated against the 7 th WHO International Standard for Rabies vaccine. The genealogy of the current Reference Standard as well as the stability programme and available stability results are described in the dossier. An acceptable protocol for qualification of future reference standards is available. Sufficient information (i.e., genealogy, qualification, period of use) has also been provided on the preceding Reference Standard that has been used for release testing of VRVg-2 step 1 FP batches.

## Batch analysis

Batch analyses results are presented for FBP batches and FP lots including the PPQ batches/lots and additional lot manufactured at Sanofi according to the proposed commercial process VRVg-2 Step 2. Release data for VRVg-2 Step 1 clinical batches and an additional stability batch are presented under 3.2.P.2.3 Manufacturing Process Development - Analytical Evolution.

All FBP batches/FP lots comply with the release specifications valid at time of release and the proposed commercial specifications. The results demonstrate that the manufacturing process is capable to deliver finished product of consistent quality that meets its specifications.

## 3.3.4. Stability of the product

## Container closure system

Final bulk product is stored in stainless steel tanks. The container closure system for FP (antigen vial) consists of a 3 mL Type I borosilicate glass vial closed with a lubricated bromo- or chlorobutyl rubber stopper and a flip-off cap made of aluminium and polypropylene. The components with product contact comply with compendial requirements (i.e., Ph. Eur. 3.2.1, and 3.2.9, respectively). The chosen CCS appears suitable in terms of compatibility, container closure integrity, and safety. The names of the suppliers are registered in the dossier and representative certificates of analysis (CoAs) are available.

The NaCl solvent is provided in a pre-filled syringe that is also used for administration of the reconstituted vaccine - a Notified Body opinion is available (please refer to the respective section of the solvent). The co-packaged sterile stainless-steel needles (with or without safety shield) in the pack

size of 1 vial and 1 pre-filled syringe are CE-marked.

## Stability data

For the freeze-dried FP, the Applicant proposes a shelf-life of 60 months at +5°C ± 3°C in the container closure described under 3.2.P.7. Stability data are provided for primary FP stability batches. Stability studies have been initiated for FP PPQ batches and additional batch manufactured at the intended commercial site using process VRVg-2

step 2

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The stability studies are conducted at long-term storage conditions (+5°C ± 3°C for up to 60 months) and accelerated conditions (up to 6 months at +25°C ± 2°C and up to 3 months at +37°C ± 2°C,

respectively). Stability of reconstituted FP (was/is evaluated after storage for up to 6 hours at +5°C ± 3°C or +22°C ± 3°C, respectively, and under in-use conditions (ambient temperature, multiple stopper punctures).

Temperature excursion studies are conducted to investigate a potential impact on product quality by exposure to +25°C ± 2°C for 1 month during long-term storage.

Photostability was evaluated using one batch that was exposed to ≥ 1.2 x 10 6 Lux hours and an integrated near ultraviolet energy of ≥ 200 watt hours/m 2 , in accordance with ICH Q1B.

The stability samples were stored in the intended commercial CCS described under 3.2.P.7.

The analytical procedures are the same as used for release testing (plus additional characterisation methods) and include stability indicating methods, including physico-chemical methods and methods for potency and safety. Results were evaluated against the specifications valid at time of testing.

In the main, the studies follow ICH Q5C and ICH Q1B; however, for several attributes the testing frequency was reduced. No specific justifications are given but under consideration of the attributes and available results, no concern is raised.

## Long-term and accelerated studies

When stored at long-term conditions, all available FP results comply with the acceptance criteria valid at time of testing and the proposed commercial acceptance criteria (except the result for G protein for one (1) primary stability batch at 48 months which was marginally below the acceptance criterion). No relevant trend is observed for any of the tested attributes.

Under both accelerated conditions (i.e., +25°C ± 2°C or +37°C ± 2°C) none of the tested parameters shows a relevant trend; all results remain within the respective acceptance criterion.

Overall, consistent stability profiles are observed for the different lots across the tested storage conditions.

## Reconstituted vaccine / In-use stability

Storage of the reconstituted vaccine for 6 hours at +2 to +25°C (single intramuscular administration) or 6 hours at +2 to +8°C (multiple intradermal administrations) had no impact on the tested quality attributes. Available results for reconstituted aged FP comply with their specifications. The approved in-use instructions are included in the product information: \"The reconstituted vaccine should be used immediately. If not used immediately, chemical and physical in-use stability has been demonstrated for 6 hours after reconstitution when stored between 2 °C and 25 °C for single administration by intramuscular route or for 6 hours in a refrigerator (2 °C - 8 °C) in case of use for multiple administrations by intradermal route. Do not freeze. After 6 hours, the reconstituted vaccine must be discarded. From a microbiological point of view, if not used immediately, in-use storage times and conditions are the responsibility of the user\"

## Temperature excursion studies

Available results for batches that had been stored for 1 month at 25°C prior to storage at long-term conditions; all results meet their specifications.

## Photostability

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

No relevant changes in product characteristics for physico-chemical methods and methods for potency were observed upon cumulative exposure to ≥ 200 watt hours/m 2 UV light and ≥ 1.2 x 10 6 Lux hours visible light, demonstrating that FP is not light sensitive.

## Advanced kinetic modelling

To further support the proposed stability claim, the Applicant used an advanced kinetic stability model (AKM) to predict product stability. No detailed information is provided on the establishment of the AKM that is based on stability data at multiple temperature conditions. However, based on the presented experimental and predicted data it seems that the model is capable to accurately predict product stability.

## Post authorisation studies

Commitments to finalise the ongoing stability studies, to perform long-term studies for at least one commercial FP batch per year, and to inform the regulatory agencies on any out of specification (OOS) results are provided. An annual stability protocol has been filed.

In line with previous discussions during the pre-submission meeting (PSM), the Applicant committed to provide post approval EOSL stability data for two additional FP batches with bromobutyl stopper and report any OOS results (Recommendation 4).

In conclusion, based on the submitted stability data the claimed FP shelf-life of 60 months at +5°C ± 3°C and the 96-hours period at up to 27°C when stored in the CCS described in 3.2.P.7 (for both types of stoppers) are agreeable. The initial concerns related to i) the comparability exercise between VRVg-2 step 1 and VRVg-2 step 2 FP, ii) the stability-indicating capability of the G protein ELISA, and iii) the missing results for particle concentration and polydispersity have been addressed.

## 3.4. Finished medicinal product - Solvent for reconstitution

## 3.4.1. Description of the product and pharmaceutical development

## Description the product

Sterile sodium chloride (NaCl) solution 0.4% is used as solvent for reconstitution of the freeze-dried VRVg product prior to administration. The solvent is supplied in a pre-filled Type I glass syringe with a luer lock (LL) adaptor, bromobutyl rubber stopper and tip cap with rigid cap and elastomeric closure. The pre-filled syringe (PFS) with solvent is terminally sterilised.

The nominal fill volume is 0.5 mL; an overfill is applied to ensure delivery of a full dose (0.5 mL) of reconstituted vaccine. The overfill is sufficiently justified by process data.

The 0.4% NaCl solution for reconstitution is a clear and colourless solution.

The composition of the solvent for reconstitution is provided in Table 4. All excipients comply with Ph. Eur.

Table 4 Composition of solvent for reconstitution

| Components           | Composition per Unit   | Function   | Reference to standards                                                            |
|----------------------|------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Sodium chloride      | 2.0 mg                 | Excipient  | Ph. Eur. Monograph 0193 USP – NF Monograph \"Sodium chloride\" JP <Sodium chloride> |
| Water for injections | q.s. 0.5 mL a          | Excipient  | Ph. Eur. monograph 0169                                                           |

a \"q.s.\" — \"Sufficient Quantity\".

A Notified Body opinion issued by TÜV Süd confirms conformity of the device parts of the PFS to the relevant GSPRs in Annex I of the Medical Devices Regulation.

## Pharmaceutical development

The 0.4% sodium chloride solution has been selected as a solvent for reconstitution based on its osmotic properties and has been registered for other freeze-dried vaccines marketed by Sanofi. No formulation development has been undertaken, with sodium chloride and water for injections being the only ingredients of the solvent.

## Manufacturing process development

Essentially, the same information on CQAs and process parameters has been filed previously for other Sanofi vaccines authorised in the EU/ EU MS (e.g. Verorab or Dengvaxia).

The Applicant identified the relevant CQAs for the 0.4% NaCl solution based on their impact on product efficacy and safety.

For each CQA, a release test or IPCT has been established. In addition, process performance attributes (PPA) were identified. The analytical control strategy appears adequate and is in line with regulatory expectations.

Based on their impact on CQAs or PPAs, process parameters were categorised as CPP, KPP, or nKPP. Summaries presenting the identified CPPs and KPPs and rationales are provided.

The six-step manufacturing process for the 0.4% NaCl solution that includes a terminal sterilisation step has previously been registered in Europe and other global markets for several freeze-dried vaccines marketed by Sanofi. The registrations included PFS without needle with integrated tip cap and PFS with attached needle and needle shield that were used in clinical studies. A new type of PFS with luer lock (LL) was selected to replace the PFS with tip cap or attached needle, respectively.

The individual manufacturing steps for final bulk solvent and PFS with solvent have been evaluated in process development studies.

The transportation process has been sufficiently validated by transportation simulation studies.

Final bulk product is stored in a sterilised, single-use bag. Suitability of the bag is supported by compendial compliance of the contact layer material, cytotoxicity studies, an extractable study, and stability data.

According to the Applicant, the container closure for the filled product is a standard packaging material used for other Sanofi vaccines. The components with product contact, i.e. Type I glass barrel, tip cap elastomer (styrene - butadiene) and plunger stopper (bromobutyl), as well as the lubricant comply with compendial requirements. Results of biocompatibility testing complied with the requirements of USP &lt;87&gt;. Extractables and leachables studies were performed for the components of the syringe. Non-targeted screening methods and targeted methods for quantitation were used to analyse the 0.4% NaCl solution for volatile, semi-volatile, and non-volatile organic compounds, products of concern, and elemental leachables. The available data do not hint at a patient risk related to leachables. Integrity and functionality of the PFS throughout shelf-life has been confirmed by CCI testing and testing of Break loose/Gliding force (BL/GF). Stability studies demonstrate compatibility of the solvent with the selected CCS. In summary, the container closure system for the solvent appears suitable regarding compatibility,

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

container closure integrity and functionality, and safety.

## 3.4.2. Manufacture of the product and process controls

Manufacturing process and controls The 0.4% NaCl solution for reconstitution is manufactured and released by Sanofi Winthrop Industrie, Val de Reuil, France. The name, address and responsibility of each manufacturer involved in solvent manufacture, testing, and batch release is described in the dossier. Valid MIAs and GMP certificates covering the performed activities are available. The manufacturing process is based on common pharmaceutical processing steps. Manufacture of the FBP includes dissolution of NaCl in WFI followed by 0.2 µm filtration. Manufacture of the filled product comprises 0.2 µm filtration, filling and stoppering of syringes, terminal heat sterilisation, and 100% visual inspection. The syringes and plungers are sterilised according to applicable ISO norms and compendial requirements. The names of the suppliers and the sterilisation sites are registered in the dossier. The final product is stored at below 25°C. The batch size is specified in the dossier. A final bulk may be filled to one or several filled product batches of variable size. Reprocessing is not described and hence, not allowed. The process description is in line with the requirements of the Guideline on manufacture of the finished dosage form EMA/CHMP/QWP/245074/2015. Critical process parameters, IPCs, and their acceptable range/acceptance criteria are listed. The identified CPPs as well as the in-process controls are consistent with regulatory expectations for this type of process and appear adequate to ensure consistent quality of FP as part of the overall control strategy. Acceptable method descriptions and validations for the in-house integrity and functional methods for IPCs on the filled PFS are available under 3.2.P.8.3. The hold time for the filled syringes prior to sterilisation is supported by respective hold time studies.

## Process validation

A suitable number of batches (through formulation, fill and terminal sterilisation) were included in process validation studies. Overall, the available process validation data in combination with the development data show that the manufacturing process for the PFS with 0.4% NaCl solvent is reliable and delivers solvent for reconstitution of adequate quality. Notably, some of the presented data have been submitted previously for other Sanofi vaccines authorised in the EU/EU MS

## 3.4.4. Stability of the product

## Container closure system

## Final bulk solution

The final bulk solution is stored in ready-to-use, sterilised single-use bags. Acceptable specifications are provided.

## Filled solvent

The primary container closure system (CCS) for the solvent consists of a 1 mL Type I glass syringe equipped with a luer lock adaptor. The syringe is closed with a rigid tip cap made of a polypropylene cap (without product contact) and a styrene-butadiene elastomer and a bromobutyl rubber stopper.

Acceptable specifications as well as drawings with the critical dimensions of the syringe barrel and the plunger stopper are provided. The syringe barrel complies with Ph. Eur. 3.2.1, tip cap elastomer and rubber stopper comply with Ph. Eur. 3.2.9.

Syringes and stoppers are sterilised by the suppliers. Names of the suppliers and site of sterilisation are provided. Compliance of the sterilisation processes with applicable ISO norms and Ph. Eur. requirements has been confirmed.

A Notified Body opinion confirming conformance of the device parts of the PFS to the relevant General Safety and Performance Requirements in Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is available.

The co-packed needles for reconstitution and administration are CE-marked.

## Stability data

Stability studies were performed at long-term conditions (+5°C ± 3°C and +25 ºC ± 2°C) and accelerated conditions (+37°C ± 2°C or +40°C ± 2°C) using filled product in syringes without attached needle with tip cap, syringes with tip cap, and syringes without attached needle with LL system (intended container closure system,). The design of the stability studies reflects the applicable requirements of ICH Q1A (no active substance is present).

The parameters include physico-chemical, content and safety tests.

The data confirmed the proposed shelf life and storage conditions for the NaCl 0.4% solution filled in syringe without attached needle with luer lock. A photostability study is not required since the NaCl solution is not photolabile.

## 3.4.5. Post approval change management protocol(s)

No post approval change management protocol has been submitted with the initial MAA.

## 3.4.6. Adventitious agents

Safety with respect to adventitious agents is ensured considering recommendations as provided in ICH Q5A. The measures set to ensure product safety with regard to non-viral and viral adventitious agents include selection of appropriate raw materials, testing of cell banks, seed lots and process intermediates for microbial and viral contaminants, testing of microbial attributes at release, and BPL virus inactivation. In addition, microbial quality is ensured by process design (microbial reduction filtrations, sterile filtration) and sanitisation procedures. Only during development of the MCB and the MSL some animal materials were used: bovine serum and porcine trypsin. EDQM certificates of suitability are available for the bovine serum which was conform with the Note for Guidance on minimising the risk of transmitting animal spongiform encephalopathy agents via human or veterinary medicinal products (EMEA/410/01). Moreover, bovine serum was irradiated and tested for adventitious viruses. Porcine trypsin was also irradiated and was tested for appropriate adventitious agents before use. The risk arising from potential TSE contaminants can be considered as negligible. Absence of contamination due to bacterial and fungal adventitious agents is controlled at various stages of production via QC release testing, in-process control and in-process monitoring testing. The risk of microbial contamination is adequately controlled. Absence of viruses in MCB, WCBs (including end-of-production cells (EOPC)), ISL, and WSL was confirmed by a battery of tests covering a broad range of viruses. For specific details and concerns refer to 3.2.S.2.3. No specific adventitious virus testing is performed on the crude harvest. However, control cells and control cell supernatants are tested for appropriate adventitious agents. This is acceptable for this type of product (inactivated viral vaccine). The contribution of the BPL virus inactivation step to clearance of adventitious viruses has been assessed in a small-scale study using four relevant model viruses. The small-scale model can be considered as representative for the commercial process. Worst-case conditions were applied in one out of the two validation runs performed. The information on relevant controls of the viral assays

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

(positive, negative, interference, cytotoxicity) has been provided.

## 3.5. Discussion and conclusions on quality aspects

Information on development, manufacture and control of the active substance has been presented. A Major objection had been raised on the AS control strategy and criticality assignment of process parameters. Results of the risk assessment performed with FMEA approach have been provided including additional details on the Process Criticality Analysis methodology and process parameter categorization as well as a detailed risk ranking score for each process parameter analysed. Based on the information provided, the classification of process parameters is considered sufficiently justified. A major objection was also raised on the AS specifications and these have now been updated as requested. The data provided on AS are now considered sufficient. Three recommendations are made: request for MCB stability data (Recommendation 1), results of completed lifetime validation studies on the purification systems (Recommendation 2) and the results for the ongoing extractables study on the flask (Recommendation 3). Information on development, manufacture and control of the finished product (freeze-dried product

and 0.4% NaCl solvent) have been presented in a satisfactory manner.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The results of tests carried out indicate satisfactory consistency and uniformity of important product quality characteristics, and these in turn lead to the conclusion that the product should have a satisfactory and uniform performance in the clinic. A recommendation is made to provide end-of-shelflife stability data for two additional FP batches with bromobutyl stopper (Recommendation 4).

A new active substance claim is not made.

## 3.5.1. Recommendation(s) for future quality development

In the context of the obligation of the MAHs to take due account of technical and scientific progress, the CHMP recommends the following points for investigation:

1. The latest available stability data for the MCB batch should be provided when a new WCB batch is manufactured (Recommendation 1).
2. The results of the completed lifetime validation studies on the purification systems at commercial scale that will be performed to support the maximum allowable number of cycles should be submitted when available. (Recommendation 2)
3. The results for the ongoing extractables study on the flask for storage and transfer of solutions should be provided by 1st half of 2027 (Recommendation 3).
4. In line with the given commitment, the Applicant should provide post approval end-of-shelf-life (EOSL) stability data for two additional FP batches with bromobutyl stopper and report any confirmed OOS results during the study. (Recommendation 4)

## 4. Non-clinical aspects

## 4.1. Introduction

The non-clinical program was first conducted to support the clinical development with VRVg-1. The non-clinical program was then updated to support Phase II dose ranging clinical trial conducted with VRVg-2.

The non-clinical pharmacology and toxicology program for VRVg was designed to demonstrate the ability of the vaccine to induce a specific and neutralizing antibody response to rabies virus and to assess its systemic and local side effects. ## 4.2. Analytical methods

Analytical methods for the quantification of the pharmacodynamic effect of the test article, namely ELISA and FAVN are considered fit for the use in non-clinical pharmacological studies.

## 4.3. Pharmacology

## 4.3.1. Pharmacodynamics

## 4.3.1.1. Primary pharmacodynamics

The applicant conducted four immunogenicity animal studies in rabbits, mice and hamsters to characterise the pharmacodynamic effects of VRVg.

Rabbit study F.RE.RAB003.Rb was conducted in preparation of the experimental conditions for future rabbit repeat dose toxicity studies. For that purpose, 4 female NZW rabbits were injected with a human dose of VRVg-2 on 6 days (0, 3, 7, 14, 28, and 42) within 8 weeks and sera were collected on 7 days (0, 3, 7, 14, 28, 42, and 56) to investigate the humoral immune response to VRVg by ELISA quantification. All rabbits displayed sustained specific antibodies after the second immunization, which increased until reaching a plateau after the fifth immunization.

Mouse study F.RE.RAB022.Ms aimed at comparing the immunogenicity of two lots VRVg vaccine prepared in an optimized process to a clinical batch which was prepared according to a previous process. Thirty groups each containing 5 female OF1 mice received two immunizations (D0 and D21) of escalating dilutions (1/5, 1/10, 1/20, 1/40, 1/80 or 1/160) of the human dose of each rabies vaccine.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Negative controls received diluent. Sera were collected on D20 and D35 and tested for rabies-specific IgG by ELISA. Neutralizing antibodies were detected by FAVN.

ELISA results prove immunogenicity of all products and no significant differences between the three VRVg products on either D20 or D35.

FAVN demonstrates induction of virus neutralizing antibodies by each product. For D20 no significant differences were observed amongst the VRVg products. The results indicate that the change in the manufacturing process did not impact the immunogenicity of VRVg.

Mouse study F.RE.RAB023 compared the immunogenicity of three VRVg batches with Verorab vaccine. Twenty-four groups each containing 5 female OF1 mice received one immunization of escalating dilutions (1/5, 1/10, 1/20, 1/40, 1/80 or 1/160) of the human dose of each rabies vaccine. Sera were collected on D14 and tested for rabies-specific IgG by ELISA. Neutralizing antibodies were detected by FAVN. In this study, all vaccines showed consistent immunogenicity and induction of rabiesneutralizing antibodies. No significant differences were detected for the tested parameters across the individual VRVg batches.

Hamster study MLE-RE-RAB-20001-Hm investigated the interference between rabies vaccine and HRIGs or ERIGs in healthy hamsters according to the Essen PEP human regimen. Six groups of 12 female Syrian Golden hamsters received 4 IM immunizations on Days 0, 3, 7 and 14 of a VRVg-2 batch combined or not with a single IM injection of HRIGs (20 IU/kg) or ERIGs (40 IU/kg)) on Day 0. Two supplementary control groups of 3 hamsters received only a single IM injection of HRIGs or ERIGs on D0. Sera were collected on D-4 (pre-test), D7, D14 and D28 to measure rabies-specific IgM by ELISA and seroneutralizing antibodies by FAVN.

In summary, this study demonstrated the immunogenicity of a GMP batch of the VRVg-2 using the Essen PEP regimen in hamsters. It also showed that the co-administration of either HRIG or ERIG at day 0 induced a transient but not significant interference on the vaccine-specific antibody response at day 7 post-immunization, but not beyond. These findings were supportive of the immunogenicity of VRVg-2 and demonstrated the interchangeability of HRIG and ERIG using a PEP regimen.
