## 5.3.6. Overall discussion and conclusions on clinical efficacy

## 5.3.6.1. Discussion

## Design and conduct of the clinical studies

The efficacy evaluation is based on the dose-ranging study VRV11 and four main Phase 3 studies: VRV12, VRV13, VRV00014 and VRV09. VRV12 and VRV13 are considered pivotal providing the confirmatory evidence through pre-specified non-inferiority analyses, while VRV00014 and VRV09 provide descriptive support for additional intramuscular and intradermal regimens. The use of RVNA ≥ 0.5 IU/mL as the principal immunogenicity threshold and the active comparators Verorab and/or Imovax Rabies are acceptable for the immunobridging strategy.

Different regimens and administrations, recommended by WHO and NITAGs and applied world-wide, were investigated in the four Phase 3 studies as explained above in main studies section.

Study VRV12 investigated an IM 3-dose PrEP regimen in paediatric and adult participants and an IM 2-dose PrEP regimen in adult participants. The 2-dose PrEP regimen in paediatric participants was also assessed. While the 3-dose PrEP schedule is still accepted by WHO, the current recommendation favours the 2-dose schedule; therefore, selecting the 2-dose regimen as the basis for the primary objective would have been more relevant and aligned with current guidance. However, at time of study planning (which was before the current Rabies vaccines: WHO position paper, April 2018 was published), the primary objective was accepted and aligned with recommendations applied at the time of study design and initial scientific advice.

Study VRV13 evaluated two IM PEP regimens, i.e., the 5-dose Essen regimen and the 4-dose Essen regimen, in adult participants.

Study VRV00014 assessed the Zagreb IM PEP regimen and Study VRV09 investigated the ID PEP regimens with paediatric and adult participants ID administration usually elicits similar immune responses but requires lower doses and is thus important when vaccine availability is critical.

Effect of booster administration was investigated in study VRV12 in two subsets of adult participants that were either primed with the 3-dose PrEP or the 2-dose PrEP regimen.

Antibody persistence was assessed in a subset of adult participants that was primed with 2 doses in study VRV12.

In all studies, selection criteria, study objectives, endpoints and sampling time points were appropriate to investigate the different regimens, as discussed in further detail below. Primary immunogenicity analyses were performed in the PPAS at relevant timepoints. This set includes only subjects from the FAS (randomized who received at least one dose) who met all protocol criteria and had no major deviations affecting the validity of the immunogenicity assessment. One of these criteria for exclusion is 'Seropositive subject at D0, i.e., RVNA titer ≥ LLOQ'. Excluding these subjects from the PPAS is considered relevant to ensure the most stringent conditions for evaluating the primary immunogenicity endpoint. Across all four Phase 3 studies, considerable numbers of participants were excluded from the per-protocol analysis sets. Studies VRV13 and VRV09 showed high rates of major deviations (47.2% and 29.4%, respectively). This was mainly due to outof-window visits or procedures, which were linked to COVID-related disruptions in both studies and a study halt (for SAE evaluation) in VRV13. This significant number of protocol deviations reduces the sample size for per-protocol analyses, having some impact on the robustness of the study results. In contrast, studies VRV00014 and VRV12 had much lower rates (≤15%), with most deviations related to randomization or missed samples. Critical deviations were rare across all studies. Albeit the percentages between the respective groups are similar and thus one might conclude that this is unlikely to affect comparative immunogenicity evaluation between the vaccine candidate and the comparators, there is still the chance that the robustness of the immunogenicity analysis could be affected (see below, baseline RVNA titers). Studies VRV12 and VRV13 had confirmatory statistical hypothesis testing approaches. Both the primary series of Cohort 1 of study VRV12 and the vaccination arms receiving VRVg-2/Verorab Rabies/Imovax Rabies in study VRV12 were observer-blinded with well-defined blind breaking criteria. Both studies were centrally randomised and the procedure for randomization was adequately described. The Applicant did not specifically define an estimand according to the framework outlined in ICH E9(R1) for their primary immunogenicity endpoint or any secondary endpoints in VRV12 or VRV13. Indeed, the implementation of the estimand framework in prophylactic vaccine trials requires specific considerations and has not been taken up consistently (see Beckers et al. \"Adopting the estimand framework in prophylactic vaccine trials\", Vaccine, Volume 64, 2025). The primary objective of the studies (non-inferiority of the antibody response) was planned to be evaluated in those participants who did not deviate from the intended prophylactic dosing regimen or violate essential protocol requirements potentially impacting immunogenicity. Any foreseen intercurrent events, although not defined as such by the Applicant, were considered protocol deviations, and any further missing data were not imputed. Since the protective effect of a prophylactic vaccine administered in healthy subjects generally cannot be perceived prior to the primary immunogenicity endpoint evaluation and since immunogenicity endpoints can be objectively measured, intercurrent events that lead to protocol deviations are unlikely to be directly influence by the vaccine efficacy or the subjects' perception of such. Therefore, there is less risk that the PPAS may be biased than in other settings. Therefore, the Applicant implicitly targeted an appropriate estimand: a clinically clearly interpretable difference in serological response to a prophylactic vaccine administered as intended in an evaluable subject set (i.e. the PPAS). The main factors that could complicate interpretation of analysis on this set would be low compliance or differential compliance between treatment arms (the latter of which was not observed), for example due to AEs associated with a specific immune response or other participant characteristics. In the case of low compliance (&lt;90%, which was observed), the Applicant planned supplementary analyses on the FAS(I), which more closely represent the full study population and are closer to the intent to treat principle. Results of this analysis, i.e. an analysis including data from participants who did not fully adhere to the protocol, could be more reflective of real-world administration of the vaccine (with the exception of the inclusion of participant data

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

EMEA/H/C/006602/0000

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

collected outside the defined sampling windows, which could make estimation of immunogenicity endpoints less precise). Overall, this approach is endorsed. The primary endpoints in the VRV12 study and in the VRV13 study were well defined. NI was considered demonstrated if the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI of the difference of the proportions (VRVg-2 minus comparator) was greater than -5%. Wilson's score test is an appropriate method for evaluating binomial proportions. The Applicant used the version without continuity correction, which generally has good average coverage but more liberal CIs near extreme proportions (which are expected in this case, given the anticipated comparable immunogenicity response between the vaccine groups). No rationale for the NI margin itself is provided that links the difference in immunogenicity to potential clinically relevant differences in vaccine efficacy, however, an allowed 5% difference in proportions is on the smaller end of typical NI margins for immunogenicity studies. Taking the two previous points together, the NI criterion is considered sufficiently stringent. It is also worth highlighting that the Applicant actually considered co-primary endpoints without explicitly stating so: They require NI to be shown for both comparisons of VRVg-2 vs. Verorab and VRVg-2 vs. Imovax in both adult and paediatric subjects in VRV12, and both non-inferiority comparisons of VRVg-2 +HRIG vs. Verorab+HRIG and VRVg-2 vs. Imovax+HRIG in VRV13. It would typically be expected that stratification variables are incorporated as covariates in an overall primary analysis (see the Guideline on adjustment for baseline covariates in clinical trials EMA/CHMP/295050/2013); in the setting of tests on binomial proportions, this could be achieved using weights. However, the Applicant's approach to considering NI comparisons in both age groups as co-primary in VRV12 is not objected to from a methodological perspective, and the lack of weighting by centre in both studies is not considered critical for invalidating a potential NI conclusion (subgroup analyses by age and centre are also provided in both studies in addition to some by race, gender, and ethnicity, which is endorsed). Overall, the methods for analysing the primary endpoint are considered acceptable. The Applicant planned to test several secondary immunogenicity endpoints in VRV12, and one key secondary immunogenicity endpoint in VRV13. They employed a fixed-sequence/gatekeeping strategy for Type I error control (at a one-sided alpha level of 0.025) in both cases: The first secondary endpoint was only permitted to be tested if the primary endpoint was met, and in VRV13 the second secondary endpoint only if the first secondary endpoint was met, and so on, proceeding down a predefined hierarchy. This strategy is considered acceptable. The first secondary immunogenicity endpoint, superiority in the overall 3-dose PrEP VRVg-2 group at D42 for VRV12 and superiority in the VRVg-2+HRIG at D28 in VRV13, is considered especially clinically relevant for generating supportive evidence for the primary endpoint. Thus, its appearance at the top of the testing hierarchy in VRV12 is endorsed. Specifically, the Applicant planned to test whether the lower bound of the 95% CI of the proportion of these subjects with RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL exceeded 97% (95% in VRV13) as calculated using the exact binomial distribution (Clopper Pearson method). While no rationale for the superiority threshold is provided it is clearly stringent. It is also not clear why the Applicant elected to use the exact binomial test with Clopper Pearson CIs - which are typically conservative - given that Wilson's method was used for the primary analysis. However, the different methods for testing binomial proportions/calculating CIs should be similar enough to not cause major concern regarding consistent interpretation of results. The planned testing approaches for the Applicant's further error-controlled secondary immunogenicity objectives in VRV12 recycle the same NI and superiority analysis methods (albeit occasionally with different margins). The final NI objective requires a GLM with binomial responses, since different time points are compared. Appropriate descriptive methods were planned for a further series of immunogenicity endpoints that were not subjected to formal testing in both VRV12 and VRV13.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Overall, the sample size calculations for both trials can be approximately followed using the software nQuery v9.3.0 and although discrepancies remain no serious concerns regarding an impact on the conclusions of the trials are raised.

The study VRV12 contains a live blinded re-estimation of the number of evaluable subjects in the PPAS (from the attrition rate) with no consequence for the number of enrolled subjects. VRV13 contains several amendments of the sample size during the ongoing study (in terms of planned number of enrolled participants) because the expected number of evaluable subjects in the PPAS decreased due to study holds (emergence of a SAE, and due to COVID-19 restrictions). Ideally, the loss of these evaluable participants would have been covered by a more accurate estimate of the attrition rate during the initial planning of the trial. While the protocol of VRV13 allows for replacements of subjects in the PPAS and an increase in sample size, if necessary, no specific implementation criteria are pre-planned in either study (as would be required). However, since the Applicant provided supplementary analyses of immunogenicity and safety data on the FAS(I) and ancillary (VRV12)/sensitivity (VRV13) analyses of the impact of COVID-19 measures on immunogenicity and safety to aid assessment, this issue is not considered critical in the specific context of this development programme.

## General observation on baseline RVNA titers

A notable proportion of participants across all trials presented with baseline RVNA titers ≥0.5 IU/mL or above the LLOQ prior to vaccination. This was most frequent in Thailand (endemic setting; VRV12, VRV00014, and VRV09), where 10.9%-11.9% of participants had baseline RVNA ≥0.5 IU/mL. However, this was also observed in non-endemic countries (France and the US; VRV13 and VRV11), where 1.7%-2.2% of participants had baseline RVNA ≥0.5 IU/mL. Individual response trajectories of participants with baseline RVNA titers ≥ LLOQ showed a consistent pattern across participants and studies. Following vaccination, a clear increase in RVNA titers was observed, followed by an overall decline over time in most individuals. This profile is consistent with an anamnestic immune response and does not indicate irregular patterns suggestive of assay artefacts. In addition, data on the longterm performance of the RFFIT assay demonstrate that assay performance remained stable throughout the clinical development programme of VaxRabeo. Taken together, these findings indicate that the observed baseline RVNA positivity is unlikely to be driven by assay-related issues and is more plausibly explained by prior Rabies vaccination. The exclusion of baseline-positive participants from the PPAS is considered an appropriate measure to mitigate any potential impact on the immunogenicity analyses.

## Dose finding (Study VRV11)

Initially, the Applicant developed VRVg-1, which was intended to replace the Applicant's rabies vaccines Verorab and Imovax Rabies, and was - like Verorab - based on Vero cells. However, after results from clinical studies VRV02 and VRV04 showed unexpectedly low immunogenicity of VRVg-1, the VRVg-1 formulation was modified to enhance the immune response by increasing the antigen amount and adding rHA as a stabilising excipient, creating VRVg-2. The Phase 2 study VRV11 investigated three different dose levels of VRVg-2 compared to Imovax Rabies and VRVg-1. A clear dose-response was observed for VRVg-2 and the Applicant eventually proceeded with the high(est) dose (targeted quantity of antigen is 9.0 IU/0.5 mL) to Phase 3, which is reasonable.

## 3-dose and 2-dose IM PrEP regimens in paediatric and adult participants (Study VRV12)

Study VRV12 met its primary objective. In addition, the first, second and third secondary objectives were achieved. The 4 th secondary objective was not achieved because the point estimate was slightly lower (98.8%, PPAS) than the success criterion (at least 99.0%). The 5 th objective was achieved, however, this analysis is of minor relevance for the purpose of the assessment of VRVg-2 because it compares two regimens of one comparator vaccine as regards their immune responses and is thus not addressed in detail. In addition, it can no longer be considered to be under Type I error control since the previous endpoint in the testing hierarchy was not significant.

Furthermore, descriptive data (RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL, RVNA GMTs, complete neutralization at serum dilution 1:5) indicate that immune responses elicited after 2 or 3 (primary) doses of VRVg-2 are at least comparable to those elicited by 2 or 3 (primary) doses of the comparators, for both the paediatric and adult participants. Immune responses of paediatric participants were in general considerably higher than those of adults, which is not unexpected as immune responses in children are usually stronger.

Booster after primary vaccination with 3-dose IM PrEP regimen (Study VRV12, adults only)

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

At Month 12 (pre-booster dose), the proportion of subjects who achieved an RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL was almost identical in Group 1 (primed with VRVg-2: 53.8%) and Group 2 (primed with Verorab: 53.8%) and considerably lower in Group 3 (primed with Imovax Rabies: 35.7%), indicating a significant waning of titres within 1 year, which was corroborated by results of RVNA GMTs and complete neutralization at serum dilution 1:5 data. However, at Day 14 after booster administration of VRVg-2 for all groups, all subjects had an RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL in all groups and RVNA GMTs increased considerably (Group 1 pre-booster GM: 0.679 vs. Group 1 post-booster GM: 56.5) demonstrating that a single booster administration elicits a sufficient (i.e., at least the protective RVNA titer threshold) anamnestic immune response.

## Booster after primary vaccination with 2-dose IM PrEP regimen (Study VRV12, adults only)

At Month 24 to Month 36 (pre-booster), the proportion of subjects who achieved an RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL was higher in Group 4 (primed with VRVg-2: 62.0%) than in Group 5 (primed with Verorab: 51.5%) but slightly lower than in Group 6 (primed with Imovax Rabies: 64.9%). There was a significant waning of immune responses within 1 year for all 3 groups, similar to data of those primed with 3 doses and also supported by RVNA GMTs and complete neutralization at serum dilution 1:5 data. However, also likewise to the 3-dose primed subjects, at Day 14 after the booster dose, a RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL was reported for all (100%) subjects in all 3 groups. Moreover, RVNA GMT data indicates elicitation of strong anamnestic immune responses upon booster administration of VRVg-2 irrespective of the Rabies vaccine (VRVg-2, Verorab or Imovax Rabies) used for primary vaccination (priming), but a considerable higher one in participants primed with VRVg-2 (VRVg-2 on top of VRVg-2, Group 4).

Of note, when comparing booster results of those primed with 3 doses compared to those primed with 2 doses, in particular GMTs (which allow a more sensitive comparison than e.g., percentages achieving a titer threshold), it is apparent that participants who received 2 doses and the single booster between 2 to 3 years after the primary vaccination had almost twice the booster response as participants who received 3 doses and the single booster 1 year after the primary vaccination (e.g., post-booster: Group 4: 95.4 vs. Group 1: 56.5; pre-booster: Group 4: 0.761 vs. Group 1: 0.679). Although it is clear that the elicited booster responses would be sufficiently protective, considering an additional elapsed time span of at least 12 months and up to 24 months in the 2-dose groups compared to the 3-dose groups and the considerable waning of RVNA titer, this observation is rather unexpected. The Applicant provided some explanations that seem plausible, supported by literature, and noted that a similar observation was made in a trial with Imovax Rabies (study VAJ00001; Quiambao et al., 2022, Vaccine). Regardless the exact reason for this observation, there is no concern about the ability of VRVg-2 to induce an adequate immune response and since the elicited RVNA titers in both groups (irrespective of priming with 2 or 3 doses and booster timing) exceeded the protective threshold considerably.

## Immunogenicity persistence after primary vaccination with 2-dose IM PrEP regimen (Study VRV12, adults only)

The proportions of subjects with an RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL declined after Day 28 to 56.7% in Group 4 (VRVg-2), 43.2% in Group 5 (Verorab), and 57.5% in Group 6 (Imovax Rabies) at Month 6, then further to 52.9% in Group 4 (VRVg-2), 43.2% in Group 5 (Verorab) 45.0% in Group 6 (Imovax Rabies) at Month 12 and to 41.2% in Group 4 (VRVg-2), 38.9% in Group 5 (Verorab), 42.1% in Group 6 (Imovax Rabies) at Month 18. That observed decline is in line with the values reported for the 3-dose regimen, e.g., Group 1 (VRVg-2) pre-booster dose at Month 12: 53.8%. However, the proportions of subjects with an RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL at the next measurement (between Month 24 and Month 36, pre-booster) were higher than all those reported prior at Months 6, 12, and 18 with measured percentages of 63.9% in Group 4 (VRVg-2), 54.1% in Group 5 (Verorab), and 65.8% in Group 6 (Imovax Rabies). A similar trend was observed in analysis of RVNA GMTs and complete neutralization at serum dilution 1:5. Considering an additional elapsed time span of at least 6 months (and up to 18 months), and the considerable waning of RVNA titer, this finding is rather unexpected. The Applicant investigated this rise but did not identify a clear root cause; potential exposure to rabid animals or additional vaccination was excluded and no laboratory deviations were detected. The Applicant hypothesized potential exposure to other members of the Lyssavirus genus but it remains unclear if such events have indeed a relevant effect, considering that such exposures are rather rare. The applied assay has a certain variability (within ± 30% range, a serological titer of 0.5 IU/ml reported from a RFFIT on one day may be reported as 0.4 or 0.6 IU/mL) but is considered adequate for the purpose of and other measurements would have likely been also affected. Consequently, the underlying reasons for the observed unexpected titer rise remains elusive; no concern arises however, as this does neither question the effect of the primary vaccination nor the booster.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Essen-4 and Essen-5 IM PEP regimen (with concomitant administration of HRIG at Day 0) (Study VRV13, adults only)

Study VRV13 met its primary objective. In addition, the secondary objective 'Superiority of IM PEP regimen (+HRIG) at Day 28', was achieved.

The reported data indicate that immune responses towards rabies elicited by VRVg-2 in the context of the Essen-4 and Essen-5 regimens (with concomitant injection of HRIG) are comparable to those elicited by Verorab and Imovax Rabies but also similar to those elicited by VRVg-2 alone (without HRIG), in adults. Moreover, analyses of proportion of subjects with RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL, RVNA GMTs, and complete neutralisation at a serum dilution of 1:5, demonstrated that RVNA titers increased with the number of doses administered, in all treatment groups.

Of note, at Day 14 (7 days after the 3 rd treatment), the timepoint advised in EMA-SA as this data is informative of the speed of achieving the protective titer threshold, the percentage of subjects with RVNA titers ≥ 0.5 IU/mL was highest in those who received VRVg-2 but without HRIG, i.e., 97.1%, which is expected. Amongst the groups in which participants received HRIG, percentage of subjects with RVNA titers ≥ 0.5 IU/mL was higher in Group 1 (VRVg-2 + HRIG) than in Group 2 (Verorab + HRIG) and slightly lower than in Group 3 (Imovax Rabies + HRIG): 92.5% in Group 1, 88.0% in Group 2, and 94.1% in Group 3, respectively.

## Zagreb IM PEP regimen (with concomitant administration of HRIG at Day 0) (Supportive Study VRV00014, adults only)

Albeit at Day 35 (14 days after the 3 rd and last treatment), the proportion of subjects with RVNA titers ≥ 0.5 IU/mL was 100% in both treatment groups, Day 35 GMTs and proportions of subjects with RVNA titers ≥ 0.5 IU/mL as well as GMTs for Days 14 and 90 indicated a trend of slightly lower immune responses towards Rabies in the VRVg-2 + HRIG group compared to the Verorab + HRIG group. This finding is in contrast to the results of studies VRV12 (2- and 3-dose IM PrEP) and VRV13 (Essen-4 and Essen-5 IM PEP), where VRVg-2-elicited RVNA titers were in general higher than Verorab-elicited RVNA titers, however, no concern is raised as the respective comparative CIs overlap.

## IPC and TRC ID PEP regimen without RIG (paediatric subjects) (Study VRV09)

RVNA data indicate that immune responses towards Rabies elicited by VRVg-2 are marginally higher than those elicited by Verorab, in the paediatric population.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## IPC and TRC ID PEP regimens with HRIG (adults) (Study VRV09)

In the context of ID administration with HRIG, although immunogenicity towards Rabies elicited by VRVg-2 (Group 5) was higher than that elicited by Verorab (Group 6) on Day 14, VRVg-2 immunogenicity towards Rabies elicited by VRVg-2 was numerically lower than that elicited by Verorab on Day 42 and Day 90. However, since CIs of Day 42 and Day 90 results overlap, this is unlikely of clinical relevance as regards the comparison.

## Unexpected low titers at Day 14 after ID PEP administration (IPC regimen, Study VRV09)

The seroprotection rates observed for the IPC regimen in adults were unexpectedly low in both the VRVg-2 group and the Verorab group, contrasting with data from study VRV13 and published Verorab studies. Study RAB40 (Quiambao et al. 2019) reported a proportion of subjects with RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL at Day 14 after 3 ID doses (as per IPC regimen + ERIG) of 98.8% and Day 14 GMTs for the FAS of 5.89 IU/mL largely exceeded the 0.518 IU/mL reported for PPAS of the Verorab group (Group 6) of study VRV09. In study RAB56 (Auerswald et al., 2023), Verorab ± ERIG as per the IPC regimen was compared to Verorab ± ERIG as per the Essen-4 regimen, in adult and paediatric participants, with ERIG administration according to necessity and blood sampling at Day 14 and Day 28. Only a minority of 13.8% of participants in study RAB56 was administered ERIG. Irrespective of ERIG administration, at Day 14 all ID subjects achieved RVNA titer ≥ 0.5 IU/mL whereas not all IM subjects did. RVNA titers at Day 14 measured with the RFFIT assay at the GCI laboratory (same as for all VRVg-2 studies) were comparable between ID and IM groups without administered ERIG and were higher for the ID+ERIG group as compared to IM+ERIG group (though 95% CI overlapped). Overall, RVNA GMTs obtained by the Applicant's RFFIT assay in study RAB56 for the ID arm (6.17 without ERIG and 7.52 IU/mL with ERIG) also largely exceeded those reported for VRV09 both for the paediatric and adult subjects. The Applicant conducted supplementary investigations at the clinical sites. No clear root cause was identified, and no deviations from operating and laboratory procedures and quality of VRVg-2 or Verorab were found at site level. However, some limitations were noted. Although personnel administering the vaccines were trained, they did not routinely perform ID injections. At the clinical site (7640003) where all adults receiving HRIG were recruited, uncertainties regarding ID administration could not be excluded because documentation of wheal or papule observation 30 minutes post-vaccination was missing. At the same site, the IMP transfer process was not documented, lacking arrival time and minimum-maximum temperature records. Additionally, albeit the Day 14 sampling proved to be sufficient in study VRV13 and also Verorab studies, sampling on Day 28 would have been optimal to conclude on early immunogenicity and because the additional dose administration on Day 28 (as per TRC regimen, 2-2-2-0-2) masks the effect of IPC regimenelicited immunogenicity. Furthermore, no other diseases or concomitant medications that might influence immune response were reported, and it was not possible to re-evaluate subjects or collect additional samples to check for comorbidities. Of note, VRV13 and VRV00014 used the same batch of VRVg-2 as VRV09, while VRV00014 used the same Verorab batch as VRV09. RVNA analyses of all VRVg-2 studies were performed at GCI. However, this may only explain the low titer results observed in adults. For the clinical site (7640002) that enrolled the paediatric participants, the investigator stated that wheals/papules were present after ID injection and the site recorded this as swelling on the worksheet at 30-minutes post vaccination assessment. When comparing Day 14 titer results (IPC regimen, Verorab) of both paediatric and adult subjects from study RAB56 (6.17 IU/mL, without ERIG) to the Day 14 titers (IPC regimen) observed in the paediatric groups of study VRV09 (VRVg-2: 2.93 IU/mL vs. Verorab: 2.56 IU/mL), it is questioned whether this considerable difference in Verorab titers at Day 14 between studies VRV09 and RAB56, despite the same regimen may be explained (only) by the fact that these are different studies with different populations. This would then also indicate that improper ID administration at site 7640003 may not be the case and were not causal for the lower titers in adults.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Although it is acknowledged that the simulated PEP conditions may have some interference effect, this is not fully agreed with as based on results of study VRV13, which investigated also a PEP regimen (IM) with RIG administration, such an effect is considered to not be of the magnitude observed in study VRV09.

However, several factors allow extrapolation from other Verorab IPC studies. VRVg-2 consistently demonstrated comparable immune responses to Verorab across studies following both IM and ID administration, as assessed by the biologically relevant RFFIT neutralisation assay. Despite differences in antigen content and purity, VRVg-2 and Verorab share similar viral particle characteristics and antigenic presentation, supporting comparable immune recognition and response.

Nevertheless, in light of the remaining uncertainty, the Applicant's conservative approach to restrict the IPC regimen to individuals below 18 years of age is acknowledged and accepted.

## IPC and TRC ID PEP regimens with ERIG (adults) (Study VRV09)

Data of the concomitant administration of the vaccines (VRVg-2 and Verorab) with ERIG are limited and only available for Day 14 (i.e., 7 days after the 3 rd dose). This is due to the Applicant's decision to discontinue the use of ERIG in study VRV09, following the reporting of 3 serious hypersensitivity events assessed as related to ERIG (2 cases in Verorab group and 1 case in VRVg-2 group) since the benefit-risk ratio of co-administration of ERIG in simulated PEP conditions in healthy participants was not deemed favourable, to which is agreed. ERIG was subsequently replaced by HRIG.

## Subgroup analyses (main studies)

Immunogenicity data as regards subgroup analyses (sex, age, centre) corroborated the results observed by the overall analyses. All Phase 3 studies enrolled participants aged 18 years and older but the amount of data in individuals ≥65 years is very limited (n = 34 overall). Elicited immune responses towards Rabies decreased with increasing age, which is not unexpected as immune responses are generally weaker with increasing age. However, protective titers were also observed in adults aged older 65, therefore no issue is raised.

## Extrapolation of booster and persistence data of adults to paediatric individuals (Study VRV12)

No booster or persistence data in paediatric participants were collected. However, given that the dosage for children and adults is identical (age-independent), the observed overall higher titres in paediatric subjects compared to adult subjects after primary vaccination, and (at least) similar immune responses after VRVg-2 booster administration irrespective of the vaccine used for priming, there is no reason to expect significantly lower immunogenicity in children than in adults as regards anamnestic immune responses.

## Extrapolation of paediatric data to individuals below 1 year of age (Study VRV12, Study VRV09)

Studies VRV12 and VRV09 enrolled paediatric participants aged 1 year and above but no data is available for those below 1 year of age; a waiver was granted by the PDCO for this age group. The Applicant explained that vaccine responses are similar across age groups for which data were gathered and therefore could be extrapolated to paediatrics below 1 year of age. Considering that official rabies PrEP and PEP vaccination schedules are for all age groups, and other rabies vaccines are also approved without age limits, the severity of the disease and the immunogenicity results for other age groups, no concern is raised and an indication for all age groups is acceptable.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Extrapolation of data to ID PrEP regimen in paediatric and adult subjects

VRVg-2 administered as per the ID PrEP regimen was not investigated and full extrapolation from Verorab is not considered justified. While such approach was supported in previous scientific advice, there was also the prerequisite of pharmaceutical comparability. However, as aforementioned, VRVg-2 and Verorab cannot be considered comparable.

However, VRVg-2 demonstrated immune responses comparable to Verorab across IM and ID studies using the RFFIT assay. Furthermore, immunogenicity data from paediatric subjects receiving the ID PEP regimen support that VRVg-2 induces the expected immune response following ID administration.

Overall, the remaining uncertainty whether the immune response to the ID PrEP regimen is indeed comparable to IM PrEP, is therefore considered negligible.

## Extrapolation of gathered data to PEP regimens with RIG in paediatric individuals

No PEP data with concomitant RIG administration are available in paediatric subjects due to ethical considerations. Nevertheless, extrapolation from adults is considered acceptable, as paediatric participants generally showed stronger immune responses than adults and VRVg-2 demonstrated comparable immunogenicity to Verorab across PEP studies. For the Essen-4, Essen-5, Zagreb and TRC regimens, high seroprotection rates and non-inferior immune responses were observed in adults receiving RIG, raising no concerns for extrapolation to children. Although lower-than-expected titres were observed with the IPC regimen in VRV09, paediatric responses remained substantially higher than adult responses, and the overall evidence does not indicate a clinically relevant concern. Therefore, extrapolation of adult PEP data with RIG to the paediatric population is considered acceptable.

## Extrapolation of data to PEP regimen with ERIG in paediatric and adult individuals

The Applicant explained that this information can be inferred from extrapolation of Verorab data to VRVg-2. However, as outlined above, ERIG data are limited. Hence, whether concomitant use of ERIG does not negatively impact immune responses elicited by VRVg-2 to a potentially clinically important extent is unclear. While HRIG is recognized as a safer alternative, ERIG continues to be used and approved in several low- and middle-income countries. The limited data for concomitant use of ERIG are acknowledged. Given the risk for hypersensitivity, further clinical studies are considered unethical, and no further issue is raised.

## Extrapolation of PEP data to previously immunized individuals (non-naïve individuals)

For previously immunized individuals, administration of 1 dose of vaccine IM (0.5 mL) or ID (0.1 mL) on Days 0 and 3 is proposed by the Applicant.

The 2-dose IM PEP schedule in previously immunized individuals was not directly evaluated with VRVg-2. Reference is made to the pivotal PrEP trial (Study VRV12), which assessed only a single booster dose. Given that a robust immune response was demonstrated in this study at 14 days after the booster dose, irrespective of primary vaccination with 3- or 2 doses IM and even after up to 3 years after (2-dose primed data). It is considered acceptable from an immunogenicity perspective to use these data as supportive evidence for the 2-dose IM PEP schedule in non-naïve individuals.

Similarly, the 2-dose ID PEP schedule in previously immunized individuals was not evaluated with VRVg-2. However, considering that, as noted above, a remaining uncertainty whether the immune response to ID PrEP is indeed comparable to IM PrEP is considered negligible and, additionally, the strong anamnestic responses to VRVg-2 booster, it is not expected that this regimen would fail to elicit protective titers.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Extrapolation of gathered data to concomitant vaccination with typhoid polysaccharide Vi vaccine

While the applicant argued that VaxRabeo could be administered concomitantly with a typhoid polysaccharide Vi vaccine, the effects of such co-administration were not investigated. Therefore, inclusion of this concomitant vaccination in the SmPC is not supported by the available data. Any claim regarding co-administration would require supportive clinical data generated with VaxRabeo (VRVg-2) and the respective concomitantly administered vaccine.

## Extrapolation of gathered data to immunocompromised individuals

Extrapolation of Verorab data to VaxRabeo is reasonable as clinical data clearly show non-inferior immune response of VaxRabeo compared to Verorab across all available studies, even though VaxRabeo and Verorab are two different vaccines, as aforementioned. Notably, it is stated in the PI that serological testing to verify the immune response of the immunocompromised individual should be performed (PrEP) or may be indicated (PEP), and official recommendations should be followed. In addition, safety and effectiveness (including vaccination failure or lack of vaccine efficacy) will be monitored by routine pharmacovigilance activities.

## 5.3.6.2. Conclusions on the clinical efficacy

The clinical efficacy of VaxRabeo is inferred from the comparative immunogenicity results from studies VRV12 and VRV13 and the supportive findings from studies VRV00014 and VRV09. The data support the proposed PrEP, PEP and booster uses, subject to the regimen-specific limitations and restrictions reflected in the product information. In summary, immunogenicity has been successfully demonstrated.

## 5.4. Clinical safety

Please refer to the table of studies in section 4.3.2.

## 5.4.1. Safety data collection

Participants were observed for 30 minutes after each vaccination for immediate unsolicited systemic AEs. Solicited injection-site and systemic reactions were recorded in diary cards on the day of vaccination and for 7 days after each vaccination; unsolicited non-serious AEs were collected for 28 days after vaccination, and SAEs and AESIs were collected until 6 months after the last vaccination.

Solicited reactions were recorded with intensity, duration and action taken and were considered related to vaccination by definition.

The integrated safety analysis included safety data from the five main clinical studies (VRV09, VRV11, VRV12, VRV13, and VRV00014) after the primary vaccination schedule (PrEP or simulated PEP), excluding booster dose. Safety data post-booster dose was described with study VRV12. The ISS also excluded adult participants who concomitantly received ERIG as the 2 corresponding groups from VRV09 were discontinued due to safety concerns linked to ERIG.

The Safety Analysis Set (SafAS) was defined as participants who received at least one of the study vaccines (including VRVg-2, Verorab, and Imovax Rabies). SafAS was used to describe safety results from each individual study according to the vaccine received on first dose.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

For the integrated safety analysis, all participants were also analysed according to the vaccine and concomitant medication (HRIG) they actually received on the first dose.

The following 9 vaccine groups were displayed in the ISS:

- \"VRVg-2\": participants who received VRVg-2 without HRIG on D0
- \"VRVg-2+HRIG\": participants who received VRVg-2 with HRIG on D0
- \"Verorab\": participants who received Verorab without HRIG on D0
- \"Verorab+HRIG\": participants who received Verorab with HRIG on D0
- \"Imovax Rabies\": participants who received Imovax Rabies without HRIG on D0
- \"Imovax Rabies+HRIG\": participants who received Imovax Rabies with HRIG on D0
- \"VRVg-2 Overall\": participants who received VRVg-2 without or with HRIG on D0
- \"Verorab Overall\": participants who received Verorab without or with HRIG on D0
- \"Imovax Rabies Overall\": participants who received Imovax Rabies without or with HRIG on D0

In each individual study and in the integrated safety analysis, the safety analyses are descriptive only. The safety analysis is displayed in the overall population and stratified by age group (paediatric participants aged 12 months through 17 years and adults aged ≥ 18 years) and by administration route (ID and IM). Subgroup analyses were also performed by gender (female/male) and by ethnicity in individual studies.

The safety database is composed of a total of 2079 participants who received at least one dose of VRVg-2: 417 paediatric participants (aged &lt; 18 years) and 1662 adults (aged ≥ 18 years).

## 5.4.3. Adverse events

## Integrated safety analysis

Overall population n: number of participants experiencing the endpoint listed in the first column; M: number of participants with available data for the relevant endpoint; Within solicited period: solicited injection site reactions from D0 to D7 after each dose; solicited systemic reactions between each dose if doses are separated less than 7 days, and up to 7 days after each dose if doses are separated by 7 days or more; Up to 28 days: Unsolicited injection site reactions from D0 to D28 after each dose; unsolicited systemic AEs between each dose if doses are separated less than 28 days, and up to 28 days after each injection if injections are separated by 28 days or more or the next injection is interrupted; During the whole primary series: from date of first vaccination (V01) to end of 6-month follow-up of the primary series; Note: The number of study vaccine injected is different depending on the study and the assigned group within the study: VRV09: 1 D dose at D0, D7 and D28 (2 ID injections for each dose, PEP); VRV11: 1 IM dose at D0, D3, D7, D14, and D28 (PEP); VRV12: 1 IM dose at D0, D7, and D28 or 1 IM dose at D0, and D7 (PrEP); VRV13: 1 IM dose at D0, D3, D7, D14, and D28 (PEP); VRV00014: 1 IM dose at D0 (2 IM injections), D7, and D21 (PEP). Contributing studies: VRV09, VRV11, VRV12, VRV13 and VRV00014

## Solicited adverse reactions

## Injection site reactions

In the integrated safety analysis of the general population (including paediatric and adult subjects), incidences for solicited injection site reactions were numerically higher after any VRVg-2 injection compared to Verorab but very similar to Imovax with 45.7% (95% CI: 43.4; 48.0), 41.5% (95% CI: 37.6; 45.4), and 46.0% (95% CI: 41.5; 50.5), respectively. In the paediatric population, solicited injection site reactions occurred generally more frequently with 62.4% (95% CI: 57.5; 67.0), 55.8% (95% CI: 47.6; 63.8), and 55.0% (95% CI: 44.7; 65.0) after any VRVg-2, Verorab, and Imovax injection, respectively.

Injection site reactions occurred more frequently after ID compared to IM vaccination across vaccine groups. After ID vaccination, reactions occurred at 56.0% (95% CI: 49.5; 62.4) in VRVg-2 group and at 57.0% (95% CI: 47.7; 66.0) in Verorab group. Imovax was not administered intradermally. After IM vaccination, reactions occurred at % 44.2% (95% CI: 41.8; 46.6) in VRVg-2 group and at 37.8% (95% CI: 33.6; 42.2) in Verorab group. Across vaccine groups, injection site tenderness/pain was the most frequent solicited injection site reaction reported for ID and IM routes. Injection site erythema and injection site swelling occurred more frequently after ID administration. Reported frequencies (CI) after VRVg-2 IM injection were: Injection site tenderness/pain 43.8% (41.4; 46.3); Injection site erythema 2.0% (1.4; 2.8); Injection site swelling 1.3% (0.8; 1.9). Reported frequencies (CI) after VRVg-2 ID injection were: Injection site tenderness/pain 41.9% (35.6; 48.4); Injection site erythema 16.6% (12.1; 21.9); Injection site swelling 22.0% (16.9; 27.8).

Most injection site reactions were of Grade 1 or 2 intensity and resolved within 3 days. Few Grade 3

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

reactions were reported after IM vaccination across vaccine groups (none after ID vaccination). All Grade 3 events in the VRVg-2 group related to injection site tenderness/pain (6/1665 subjects, 0.4%). The Grade 3 solicited injection site reactions did not lead to study discontinuation and resolved spontaneously within 8 days. Onset and duration of injection site reactions were overall comparable between the vaccine groups.

## Systemic reactions

Overall, incidences of solicited systemic reactions were higher after VRVg-2 compared to Verorab but similar to Imovax with 42.4% (95% CI: 40.2; 44.7); 34.2% (95% CI: 30.5; 38.1), and 42.5% (95% CI: 38.0; 47.0), respectively. Systemic reactions occurred at comparable frequencies after IM and ID vaccinations. In paediatric subjects, solicited systemic reactions occurred at slightly higher frequencies compared to adults with 48.4% (95% CI: 43.6; 53.4), 35.1% (95% CI: 27.6; 43.2), and 45.0% (95% CI: 35.0; 55.3) after any VRVg-2, Verorab, and Imovax injection, respectively.

In participants aged ≥ 2 years (including adult subjects), myalgia was the most frequently reported solicited systemic reaction in all groups followed by headache and malaise. For VRVg-2, the following frequencies were reported: myalgia 33.2% (31.1; 35.4), headache 21.3% (19.5; 23.2) and malaise 18.3% (16.6; 20.1). Fever was reported in 3.3% (2.6; 4.2), 2.4% (1.3; 3.9) and 1.6% (0.7; 3.2) of participants after VRVg-2, Verorab or Imovax, respectively.

The 12-23 months groups were small (n = 19, 3, and 2 participants for VRVg-2, Verorab, and Imovax Rabies, respectively). After VRVg-2, crying abnormal and irritability were the most frequently reported systemic reactions (both 47.4%) followed by vomiting and drowsiness (both 21.1%) and appetite lost (15.8%) according to the integrated analysis. Fever was not depicted separately for this age group in the integrated analysis. In studies VRV12 and VRV9, the incidence of fever in subjects 12-23 months of age was 31.6% (6/19 subjects) after vaccination with VRVg-2 (Verorab: 1/3 subjects; Imovax: 0/2 subjects). In paediatric subjects ≥2 years of age, fever was reported in 10.6% (7.8; 13.9), 5.8% (2.7; 10.8), and 3.0% (0.6; 8.5) of participants in VRVg-2, Verorab, and Imovax Rabies groups, respectively.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Onset and duration of solicited systemic reactions were similar between the vaccine groups. Most of the solicited systemic reactions were of Grade 1 or Grade 2 intensity and resolved within 3 days after vaccination. Across all ages, few Grade 3 systemic reactions were reported across vaccine groups (&lt;2%). None of the Grade 3 reactions led to study discontinuation. Grade 3 events after VRVg-2 were mostly fever, headache and myalgia. Slightly higher frequencies of Grade 3 systemic reactions were observed after VRVg-2 compared to Verorab and Imovax across all ages. In paediatric subjects, Grade 3 systemic reactions were reported in 3.6% (95% CI: 2.0; 5.9), 0.6% (95% CI: 0; 3.6), and 1.0% (95% CI: 0; 5.4) of participants in VRVg-2, Verorab, and Imovax groups, respectively. Notably, the incidence of Grade 3 fever was higher after VRVg-2 compared to Verorab and Imovax in paediatric subjects with 1.9% (0.8; 3.8), 0.6% (0; 3.6) and 0%, respectively. Across all ages, most of the Grade 3 reactions resolved within 1 to 8 days (mainly without action taken according to the applicant). Grade 3 reactions that did not resolve within 8 days were associated with unclear temporal plausibility and alternative aetiologies such as influenza virus infection.

## Unsolicited adverse events

## Immediate unsolicited AEs/ARs (within 30min after vaccination)

Immediate unsolicited AEs were reported in 4 adult participants (0.2% across all ages) after VRVg-2 IM injections (PTs: Presyncope and Syncope, 2 cases each) in one study (VRV13). The AEs were considered by the investigator to be not related to the vaccine (but to the vaccination procedure). All cases were of Grade 1 or Grade 2 intensity and resolved spontaneously within 1 day. All events were reported after the first injection. In addition, 3 out of 4 cases also received HRIG.

## Unsolicited adverse events/reactions within 28 days

Incidences of unsolicited AEs were numerically higher after VRVg-2 compared to Verorab and Imovax with 23.1% (95% CI: 21.3; 25.1), 20.3% (95% CI: 17.3; 23.7), and 22.4% (95% CI: 18.8; 26.3), respectively. In paediatric subjects, unsolicited AEs occurred slightly less frequently compared to the overall population with numerically higher incidences after VRVg-2 compared to Verorab and Imovax with 19.9% (95% CI: 16.2; 24.1), 18.7% (95% CI: 12.9; 25.8), and 14.0% (95% CI: 7.9;

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 22.4), respectively.

Across vaccine groups, unsolicited AEs were mainly reported in the SOC of \"Infections and infestations\". Infections and infestations occurred after VRVg-2 in 9.8% (8.5; 11.2), after Verorab in 9.4% (7.3; 12.0) and after Imovax in 8.6% (6.3; 11.5) of vaccinated subjects. The following frequencies (CI) of other SOCs were reported. Gastrointestinal disorders after VRVg-2: 4.1% (3.3; 5.1), Verorab: 2.4% (1.3; 3.9) and Imovax: 4.7% (3.0; 7.0). General disorders and administration site conditions after VRVg-2: 3.3% (2.5; 4.2), Verorab: 3.1% (1.9; 4.8) and Imovax: 4.9% (3.2; 7.2). Nervous system disorders (including headache) after VRVg-2: 3.1% (2.4; 4.0); Verorab: 1.4% (0.7; 2.7) and Imovax: 2.7% (1.4; 4.5). Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders after VRVg-2: 2.1% (1.5; 2.8), Verorab: 2.7% (1.6; 4.3) and Imovax: 2.5% (1.3; 4.3).

Unsolicited ARs (AEs considered related by the investigator) occurred at comparable rates but slightly more often after VRVg-2 compared to Verorab and slightly less often compared to Imovax with 2.5% (95% CI: 1.8; 3.3), 1.9% (95% CI: 1.0; 3.3), and 3.1% (95% CI: 1.7; 5.0), respectively. Injection site haematoma, injection site pruritus, injection site bruising, fatigue, chills, abdominal pain and diarrhoea were the most frequently reported PTs occurring in 0.2-0.5% of subjects. Unsolicited AEs were mainly of Grade 1 intensity and resolved within 7 days. There were no Grade 3 unsolicited AEs after VRVg-2.

## Study VRV12 - Booster vaccination

Safety data after booster vaccination (study VRV12) was not included in the integrated analysis. Booster vaccination was performed at month 12 (Groups 1-3) or at month 24-36 (Group 4-6) after primary vaccination respectively. Primary vaccination consisted of 3 injections in the 12-month group and 2 injections in the 24-36 months group which limits the comparison of the different booster intervals. No immediate unsolicited AEs, no AESIs and no deaths were reported after Booster vaccination with VRVg-2. Solicited systemic reactions After M12 VRVg-2 booster, the observed incidences of solicited systemic reactions were 30.9% (95% CI: 21.7; 41.2) in participants primed with VRVg-2, 35.5% (95% CI: 19.2; 54.6) in participants primed with Verorab, and 46.9% (95% CI: 29.1; 65.3) in subjects primed with Imovax. After M24-36 VRVg-2 booster, the observed incidences of solicited systemic reactions were 8.6% (95% CI: 4.4; 14.9) in participants primed with VRVg-2, 2.4% (95% CI: 0.1; 12.9) in participants primed with Verorab, and 0% in subjects primed with Imovax. Myalgia followed by malaise and headache were the were the most frequently reported solicited systemic reactions after Booster vaccination. There were only 2 Grade 3 events. After M12 VRVg-2 booster, one participant (1.1%) primed with VRVg-2 showed a Grade 3 solicited systemic reaction (malaise) which occurred on D02 and resolved on D10 with medication. After M24-36 VRVg-2 booster, one participant (0.8%) primed with VRVg-2 showed a Grade 3 solicited systemic reaction (malaise) after booster dose. The subject also required hospitalization in the context of a SAE (PT: Influenza) which is acknowledged. Unsolicited adverse events/reactions After booster vaccination, unsolicited adverse events occurred in up to 15% of subjects. The most frequently reported unsolicited AEs were in the SOCs of \"Infections and infestations\", \"Gastrointestinal disorders\" and \"Nervous system disorders\", reminiscent of the data obtained after primary vaccination. There were 2 unsolicited ARs after the M24-36 VRVg-2 booster (PTs: Injection site pruritus and Rash) reported in 2 participants (1.6%). No Grade 3 unsolicited ARs were reported and no unsolicited AE led to study discontinuation after M12 or M24-36 booster vaccination.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Serious Adverse events

Following VRVg-2 booster dose (study VRV12), 7 participants experienced SAEs. None of the SAEs was considered related to vaccination with VRVg-2 by the investigator. All SAEs resolved and none led to study discontinuation.

After M12 VRVg-2 booster, a total of 3 non-related SAEs occurred in 3 participants - all during the 6-month follow-up period (from 29 days after booster exposure to end of 6 months follow-up postbooster). After M24-36 VRVg-2 booster, a total of 6 non-related SAEs occurred in 4 participants. Only 1 case (PT: Influenza) occurred during the active phase (between date of booster dose and 28 days after booster dose).

## 5.4.4. Adverse events of special interest, serious adverse events and deaths, other significant events

There were no deaths and no AESIs reported during the whole primary series.

After primary vaccination, the frequency of SAEs was comparable between vaccine groups with 27 SAEs were experienced by 26 participants (1.4% [95% CI: 0.9; 2.0]) in the VRVg-2 group, 11 SAEs by 10 participants (1.6% [95% CI: 0.8; 2.9]) in the Verorab group and 6 SAEs by 6 participants (1.2% [95% CI: 0.5; 2.7]) in the Imovax group until 6 months after last injection. No notable imbalances in terms of SOC were observed between vaccine groups. SAE numbers after VRVg-2 were mainly driven by the SOCs \"infections and infestations\" and \"Injury, poisoning and procedural complications\" (16/26 participants reporting SAEs). During the active phase (between D0 and D28) SAEs were reported in 10 subjects after VRVg-2 vaccination. None of the reported SAEs after VRVg-2 injection were considered by the investigator to be related to the vaccine.

Ten SAEs occurred within 28 days after vaccination in the VaxRabeo group (5 in children, 5 in adults): all were considered as not related to vaccine.

## 5.4.5. Discontinuation due to adverse events

Across the 5 clinical studies, 3 subjects were discontinued due to AEs after VRVg-2 during the active phase (until 28 days after vaccination). In 2 subjects, unsolicited AE PT: Exposure to communicable disease (suspected exposure to rabies; WHO Category 2) was reported. Both cases occurred after the second vaccine dose and were Grade 1 AEs considered not related to study vaccination.

In 1 adult subject in study VRV13, 2 unsolicited ARs (PTs: Abdominal pain and Diarrhoea) were reported. The subject reported Grade 2 abdominal pain and Grade 2 diarrhoea one day after second vaccine injection leading to study discontinuation. Both AEs were non-serious systemic unsolicited AEs and considered related to study vaccine. Abdominal pain and Diarrhoea resolved on day 6 with medication. The subject discontinued study vaccination.

## Age

Paediatric and adult populations were evaluated separately in the integrated safety analysis (see above).

## Gender

Paediatric participants (ISS)

Overall, the observed percentages of participants who reported at least one solicited reaction were 72.3% (95% CI: 65.8; 78.2) in females versus 70.1% (95% CI: 63.3; 76.3) in males. Injection site reactions occurred in 66.2% [95% CI: 59.4; 72.5] versus 58.3% [95% CI: 51.2; 65.2] in females and males and systemic reactions in 46.6% [95% CI: 39.6; 53.7] versus 50.2% [95% CI: 43.3; 57.1], respectively).

The observed percentages of participants who reported at least one Grade 3 reaction in females and males were 0.9% [95% CI: 0.1; 3.4] versus 1.0% [95% CI: 0.1; 3.5] for Grade 3 injection site reactions, respectively; 2.8% [95% CI: 1.0; 6.0] versus 4.4% [95% CI: 2.0; 8.2] for Grade 3 systemic reactions, respectively.

## Adult participants (ISS)

The observed percentages of participants who reported at least one solicited reaction were in females (56.2% [95% CI: 53.0; 59.3]) and in males (43.5% [95% CI: 39.2; 47.9]) after VRVg 2 injection. Injection site reactions occurred in 45.3% [95% CI: 42.1; 48.5] versus 33.2% [95% CI: 29.2; 37.4] in females and males and systemic reactions occurred in 44.6% [95% CI: 41.4; 47.8] versus 33.8% [95% CI: 29.7; 38.0], respectively.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The observed percentages of participants who reported at least one Grade 3 reaction were in both females and males 0.1% [95% CI: 0; 0.6] versus 0.2% [95% CI: 0; 1.1] for Grade 3 injection site reactions and 1.5% [95% CI: 0.8; 2.4] versus 0.8% [95% CI: 0.2; 1.9] for Grade 3 systemic reactions, respectively.

## Ethnicity

## Paediatric participants (ISS)

No safety analysis by race was conducted as all paediatric participants from VRV09 and VRV12 were Asian.

## Adult participants (ISS)

The observed percentages of participants who reported at least one solicited reaction were in White participants 62.5% [95% CI: 57.9; 67.0] and in Asian participants 46.8% [95% CI: 43.6; 49.9]. Solicited systemic reactions occurred in 50.8% (95% CI: 46.1; 55.4) of White participants who reported at least one of these reactions and in 36.1% (95% CI: 33.1; 39.1) of Asian participants.

The observed percentages of participants who reported at least one Grade 3 reaction in White and Asian participants 1.1% [95% CI: 0.4; 2.5] versus 1.2% [95% CI: 1.6; 2.1], respectively.

Numerical difference in terms of reactogenicity between White and Asian participants was observed with all the 3 vaccines.

## Pregnancy and Lactation

The use of VRVg-2 was not studied in pregnant participants.

Although pregnancy was an exclusion criterion in all clinical studies within VRVg-2 CDP and pregnancy testing was performed before each injection, the vaccine was inadvertently administered to participants who were not aware of their pregnancy or who became pregnant shortly after.

For the purposes of the analysis, the pregnancies were classified in 3 categories:

- The pregnancy was considered as \"exposed to the study vaccine when the participant was pregnant\" if the participant received the injection at any time between 7 days after their Last Menstrual Period (LMP, when LMP date was reported) or 7 days before the Estimated Date of Conception (EDC, based on ultrasonographic estimations when date of LMP was not reported) (conservative risk window) and the end of pregnancy.
- The pregnancy was considered as \"exposed to the study vaccine but not yet pregnant\" if the participant received the injection during the interval between 30 days before their LMP and 7 days after their LMP (which also corresponds to the period between 44 days and 7 days before EDC in participants for whom LMP date was not reported).
- All other pregnancies were considered as \"unexposed\".

A total of 9 pregnancies were reported in participants who had received VRVg-2 across clinical studies: 1 case in VRV11, 7 cases in VRV12, and 1 case in VRV00014. There were no pregnancies reported in VRV09 and VRV13.

Among the 9 pregnancy cases:

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- 3 pregnancy cases were considered as \"exposed to VRVg-2 when the participant was pregnant\", 2 with normal pregnancy outcome and 1 with unknown pregnancy outcome as the participant was not willing to provide any information and withdrew consent from the study.
- 2 pregnancy cases were considered as \"exposed to VRVg-2 but not yet pregnant\", 1 with normal pregnancy outcome and 1 with child details unavailable but no AEs reported neither during pregnancy nor during labor.
- 4 pregnancy cases considered as \"unexposed to VRVg-2\" (i.e., vaccinated at least 30 days before LMP). Among them, 1 reported abnormal pregnancy outcome (following tubal pregnancy assessed as not related to study vaccine), and 2 normal pregnancy outcomes (both after caesarean section with, for one of them, an episode of preterm labor without delivery assessed as not related to the study vaccine), and 1 pregnancy which was ongoing at the time of report.

No data were collected in lactating participants.

## 5.4.7. Immunological events

ADAs are not relevant for vaccines. For recorded immunological events see section 5.4.8 below.

## 5.4.8. Safety related to drug-drug interactions and other interactions

Interaction with rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)

RIG is derived from human blood (HRIG) or equine blood (ERIG).

Safety data with or without HRIG coadministration on D0 have been generated in the adult population in VRV11, VRV13, VRV09, and VRV00014. These safety data were pooled in the integrated safety analysis and displayed per vaccine group (i.e., VRVg-2, VRVg-2 + HRIG, Verorab, Verorab + HRIG, Imovax Rabies, Imovax Rabies + HRIG) as presented above.

The observed percentages of participants who reported at least one solicited reaction after any VRVg 2 injection were when HRIG was co-administered (58.0% [95% CI: 54.1; 61.8]) compared to without HRIG (46.7% [95% CI: 43.2; 50.1]). Solicited injection site reactions were reported in 43.7% (95% CI: 39.9; 47.5) versus 38.9% (95% CI: 35.6; 42.3) of participants with and without HRIG, respectively. Solicited systemic reactions: (47.1% [95% CI: 43.3; 51.0] versus 35.6% [95% CI: 32.4; 39.0], with and without HRIG, respectively. Notable differences in frequent solicited systemic reactions were: Headache (27.0% [95% CI: 23.6; 30.5] versus 16.8% [95% CI: 14.4; 19.6], respectively) and Myalgia (36.1% [95% CI: 32.5; 39.9] versus 28.6% [95% CI: 25.5; 31.8], respectively). These solicited reactions were mostly of mild intensity and short duration. Rates of Grade 3 solicited reactions were low in both groups (≤ 1.5% of participants). A higher percentage of participants reporting solicited reactions was also observed in vaccine groups with HRIG compared to those without HRIG for the comparator vaccines after any injection.

Safety data supporting the coadministration with ERIG in the adult population were planned to be generated in VRVg-2 CDP in study VRV09. Enrolment in the two vaccine groups co-administered with ERIG was halted by the Sponsor following the report of a cluster of 3 SAEs of hypersensitivity (1 case in VRVg-2 + ERIG and 2 cases in Verorab + ERIG). At that time, 26 participants had been included in VRVg-2 + ERIG group and 14 participants had been included in Verorab + ERIG group.

## 5.4.11. Overall discussion and conclusions on clinical safety

## 5.4.11.1. Discussion

## 5.4.11.1.1. Overall assessment of available safety data

Across the clinical programme, 2,079 participants received at least one dose of the final VRVg-2 formulation, of whom 417 were paediatric participants. The integrated primary-series safety analysis supporting SmPC section 4.8 included 1,906 VaxRabeo recipients and excluded booster-only exposure and participants who received ERIG; booster safety from VRV12 was assessed separately. 1,665 participants received VaxRabeo by IM route (1,360 adults and 305 children including 17 children 12 months to 23 months of age) and 241 participants received VaxRabeo by ID route (129 adults and 112 children including 2 children 12 months to 23 months of age). Safety collection covered immediate events, 7-day solicited reactions, 28-day unsolicited events and SAEs/AESIs through 6 months. The methods and descriptive analyses are considered adequate.

The predefined solicited reactions and the applied severity grading are acceptable. All solicited reactions were assessed as causally related to vaccination which is endorsed.

Safety analyses were performed separately in each of the clinical studies for VRVg-2 and the comparator vaccines. In addition, an integrated safety analysis (across all ages and separately for paediatric [&lt;18 years of age] and adult subjects [≥18 years of age]) was conducted that includes AEs after any dose from all 5 studies with or without HRIG co-administration. An evaluation after each dose was not performed in the integrated analysis but such information can be found in the individual study reports where no concerning pattern was identified between vaccine groups. Co-administration with ERIG and HRIG is discussed separately. Individual studies and the integrated safety analysis were evaluated descriptively which is accepted. Overall, the collection and evaluation of safety data can be considered appropriate. The baseline characteristics were sufficiently well balanced between vaccine groups in both age cohorts of the integrated safety analysis. However, participants were mainly female (~60%) and of Asian origin (~75%). Paediatric participants had a mean age of ~9 years and adult subjects had a mean age of ~40 years. The ISS included 1906 participants who were vaccinated with VRVg-2: 417 paediatric participants (112 ID route, and 305 IM route); 1489 adult participants (129 ID route with HRIG and 1360 IM route including 535 with HRIG). Overall, the size of the safety database and the length of the followup are considered sufficient for an evaluation of the benefit risk balance, but rare events (occurring in less than 1000 subjects) may not have been recorded. Passive post marketing surveillance is considered sufficient.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Integrated safety analysis

## Solicited adverse reactions

An acceptable reactogenicity profile in terms of solicited adverse reactions was observed after IM and ID administration of VRVg-2 (Vaxrabeo) that was overall comparable to approved rabies vaccines. The slightly higher frequency of solicited adverse reactions in the paediatric population is not of concern and a common observation for vaccines.

Unsolicited adverse events:

Overall, no clinically relevant differences were observed with the reported unsolicited adverse events between vaccine groups, and no concerning safety signals were identified.

4 adult participants reported Presyncope and Syncope, 2 cases each after VRVg-2 IM injections and were considered related to vaccination procedure by the investigator. Taken together, the warning in SmPC section 4.4 on anxiety-related reactions sufficiently addresses the potential occurrence of syncope in temporal relationship with vaccination.

Incidences of all unsolicited AEs (until up to 28 days after vaccination) and unsolicited AEs considered related to study injection by the investigator can be considered comparable between the vaccine groups despite numerical differences.

No deaths or AESIs were reported during the clinical studies. None of the SAEs reported after vaccination with VRVg-2 were considered related to the vaccine due to alternative aetiology, lack of mechanical or temporal plausibility.

Immediate unsolicited AEs/ARs (within 30min after vaccination) Unsolicited adverse events/reactions within 28 days Serious adverse events Discontinuation due to AEs

Across the 5 clinical studies, 3 subjects were discontinued due to AEs after VRVg-2 during the active phase. In 2 subjects, unsolicited adverse event PT: Exposure to communicable disease were considered not related to study vaccination. In 1 adult 2 unsolicited AEs (PTs: Abdominal pain and Diarrhoea), both grade 2, were reported. Both AEs were non-serious systemic unsolicited AEs and considered related to study vaccine. Both PTs are listed as possible ADRs in SmPC section 4.8. Subgroup analyses The database of some Age subgroup analyses for infants and the elderly after VRVg-2 vaccination are based on a limited sample size (e.g. 19 subjects were 12-24 months of age; 74 subjects were ≥65 years of age). Observed percentages of participants reporting solicited AEs tended to decrease in older age groups which is not an unusual finding. Overall, the safety profile of VRVg-2 was comparable to the comparator vaccines across age groups. Particularly among adult subjects, the incidences of solicited ARs were higher in female participants which has been observed previously in clinical studies with vaccines. Also, incidences of solicited ARs were higher in White compared to Asian subjects. At least partially, this finding may be explained by an overall increased number of injections administered to White compared to Asian subjects as studies conducted in France and US tested 5-dose regimens while Studies conducted in Thailand tested 2-, 3-, and 4-dose regimens. Since pregnancy and lactation was not investigated in the clinical studies with VRVg-2, a very limited amount of data in pregnant subjects is available which limits possible conclusions for this population. Overall, 9 pregnancies were reported in participants vaccinated with VRVg-2 across clinical studies. No concerns emerge from the provided narratives. The definitions of the applicant to define exposed pregnancies based on the dates of vaccination and last menstrual bleeding are acceptable. Accordingly, only 3 pregnancy cases can be considered as \"exposed to VRVg-2 when the participant was pregnant\" (2 normal pregnancy outcomes, 1 consent withdrawn). The current SmPC recommendations for use/non-use during pregnancy of VRVg-2 are considered appropriate. Co-administration of rabies immunoglobulins Safety data with or without HRIG co-administration on D0 were obtained in the adult population Incidences of solicited reactions after any VRVg-2 injection were higher when HRIG was coadministered compared to VRVg-2 alone. Such differences were also observed with comparator vaccines. In the VRVg-2 group, solicited injection site reactions were reported in 43.7% and 38.9% of participants with and without HRIG, respectively. Solicited systemic reactions were reported in 47.1% and 35.6% with and without HRIG, respectively). Therefore, both types of solicited adverse reactions contribute to the overall increased incidences of solicited events. As could be expected, particularly systemic reactions occurred more frequently after HRIG co-administration. Specifically, incidences of headache (27.0% vs. 16.8%) and myalgia (36.1 vs. 28.6) were increased. Grade 3 solicited reactions were reported in 1.5 % and 1% of participants with and without HRIG, respectively. In addition, no clinically significant differences were identified for VRVg-2-HRIG co-administration in comparison to approved rabies vaccines when the reactogenicity of after specific doses is reviewed in the individual study data. Therefore, HRIG co-administration can be considered safe for use in rabies PEP vaccination schedules. Safety data for co-administration with ERIG was obtained. However, enrolment in the two vaccine groups co-administered with ERIG was stopped following the report of 3 SAEs of hypersensitivity considered as related to study vaccines + ERIG. Overall, only 26 participants were included in VRVg-2 + ERIG group and 14 participants were included in Verorab + ERIG group which limits possible conclusions on ERIG co-administration.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

It appears likely that the foreign horse-derived antibodies were the cause of the reported hypersensitivity reactions based on the clustering and the provided narratives. However, as hypersensitivity reactions can generally occur after vaccination, an amended general warning regarding hypersensitivity was included in SmPC section 4.4 upon request.

## Booster vaccination

Booster vaccination was performed 12 or 24-36 months after primary vaccination respectively. No immediate unsolicited AEs, no AESIs and no deaths were reported after Booster vaccination with VRVg-2.

Overall, a comparable safety profile was observed after booster vaccination with VRVg-2 after primary vaccination with the different rabies vaccines (VRVg-2, Verorab and Imovax Rabies, respectively). Solicited adverse reactions tended to be lower compared to primary vaccination and tended to decrease with a prolonged time interval before booster vaccination. However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as the number of primary doses preceding booster differed at M12 and M24-36. Nevertheless, the decision for the necessity and timing of booster vaccinations against this deadly disease should rather be informed through considerations regarding the individual exposure risk, individual antibody levels as well as local recommendations (see also Clinical efficacy discussion).

## 5.4.11.2. Conclusions on clinical safety

Across the clinical programme, 2,079 participants received at least one dose of the final VRVg-2 formulation, of whom 417 were paediatric participants.

No clinically significant differences were observed between the treatment groups with respect to the pattern of solicited and unsolicited ARs. No Deaths or AESIs were reported in the 5 clinical studies, and no notable SAEs were recorded in close temporal relationship with VRVg-2 vaccination.

Overall, an acceptable safety profile was observed after vaccination with VRVg-2 that is comparable to approved rabies vaccines across age groups, administration routes and different PrEP/PEP schedules.

## 7.2. Periodic safety update reports (PSURs) submission requirements

Based on the fact that VaxRabeo differs in some aspects from that of previous rabies vaccines, especially its manufacturing process has changes towards a serum-free, purified Vero cell rabies vaccine (PVRV Next Generation [PVRV-NG]), and therefore, its safety profile may vary from that of previous rabies vaccines, PRAC is of the opinion that a separate entry in the list of Union reference dates (EURD list) for VaxRabeo is needed, as it cannot follow the already existing entry for rabies vaccine. The requirements for submission of periodic safety update reports for this medicinal product are set out in the Annex II, Section C of the CHMP Opinion. The applicant did not request the alignment of the new PSUR cycle with the international birth date (IBD). The new EURD list entry will therefore use the European birth date (EBD) to determine the forthcoming Data Lock Points.
